title: Reading the Moon: where day meets night, why half Moons show mountains, and how to predict any phase

summary.text: The full Moon is the brightest night of the month, yet it is the worst night to look for mountains and craters. A half Moon, which looks dimmer, shows them best. The reason is where the light comes from. The line where the Moon's day meets its night is where shadows are longest, and shadows are what show shape. Your child lights a dough Moon from three directions and counts craters, finds out how much later the Moon rises each night, and uses a bindi on a window to measure how wide the Moon is. They also learn a rule to predict any phase from the Moon's age, see why tides follow the Moon, and find out how India's Chandrayaan-3 was timed to land at lunar dawn.
summary.art: A half Moon with long dark shadows inside craters along the line between light and dark, next to a flat-looking full Moon.

intro.hook: You have a pair of binoculars and one night to look at the Moon's mountains and craters. Do you pick the full Moon, which is the brightest, or a half Moon, which looks dimmer? Most people pick the full Moon. Galileo found out in 1609 that the half Moon is the better choice.
intro.text: The edge between the Moon's lit part and its dark part is called the terminator. Along it, the Sun is low over the Moon's land, like early morning, and every bump throws a long shadow. At full Moon the Sun shines straight down on the Moon from behind us, and there are almost no shadows at all. In this unit you test this with a dough Moon and a torch. You also learn to predict the Moon's phase, find out when it rises, and measure how wide it is with a bindi.
intro.art: A child at a window with binoculars, looking at a half Moon whose craters show dark shadows along its edge of day and night.

outcomes: I can explain what the terminator is and why shadows along it show the Moon's mountains and craters.
I can explain why a full Moon is a poor night for seeing the Moon's surface, and a half Moon is a good night.
I can use the Moon's age to say its phase, and to say roughly when it rises and sets.
I can explain why the Moon's day is about 14 Earth days of sunlight and 14 of darkness, and what that means for a lander such as Chandrayaan-3.
I can measure how many Moon-widths away the Moon is, using a small disc on a window, and use the answer to work out how wide the Moon is.
I can explain why the Moon makes tides, why there are two high tides each day, and why the biggest tides come at new Moon and full Moon.
I can explain why a crescent looks different in different places, and tell how Galileo found mountains on the Moon.

terms.meaning: The line between the lit part of the Moon and its dark part. On the Moon it is the place where it is sunrise or sunset.
terms.example: On a half Moon the terminator is a straight line down the middle of the Moon.
terms.art: A half Moon with a straight line down the middle marking the edge of the light.

terms.meaning: One day and night on the Moon, from one sunrise to the next. It lasts about 29 and a half Earth days.
terms.example: Near the Moon's equator a place has about two weeks of sunlight and then about two weeks of darkness.
terms.art: A Moon with a bright half and a dark half and a long arrow going round it.

terms.meaning: Sunrise on the Moon, when the terminator passes a place and the Sun first comes up over its horizon.
terms.example: Chandrayaan-3 landed at lunar dawn, with the Sun low in the sky.
terms.art: A small lander on grey ground with the Sun just above the horizon and long shadows.

terms.meaning: The number of days since the last new Moon.
terms.example: A Moon that is 7 days old is a half Moon, lit on the right when seen from India.
terms.art: A calendar page with a new Moon on day 0 and growing shapes along the days.

terms.meaning: The time from one new Moon to the next. It is about 29 and a half days.
terms.example: The Indian calendar's lunar month is a synodic month, about 29 or 30 days.
terms.art: A ring of eight Moon shapes with a note, 29 and a half days.

terms.meaning: Light that comes in at a low angle, nearly sideways, so that every bump throws a long shadow.
terms.example: The Sun late in the afternoon gives slanting light, and shadows grow long.
terms.art: A tall tree with a very long shadow in the evening sun.

terms.meaning: The bright, rough, high ground of the Moon. It is covered in craters and is older than the dark plains.
terms.example: The bright parts of the Moon that we see are mostly highlands.
terms.art: A grey rough landscape of crowded craters.

terms.meaning: The dark, flat plains on the Moon. Maria is the Latin word for seas. They are lava that flooded out long ago, and not water. One plain is a mare.
terms.example: The dark patches that people see as a hare or a face are maria.
terms.art: A Moon with big dark patches labelled as lava plains.

terms.meaning: A round bowl-shaped hole in the Moon's ground, made when a rock from space hit it.
terms.example: A crater has a raised rim and may have a peak in its middle.
terms.art: A round crater cut in half to show a bowl, a rim and a central peak.

terms.meaning: A simple rule that gives a good guess, but is not exact.
terms.example: The rule that the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day is a rule of thumb.
terms.art: A hand holding a thumb up beside a clock.

terms.meaning: The slow rise and fall of the sea each day, caused mainly by the Moon's pull.
terms.example: On a beach in Chennai, the water edge moves in and out twice a day.
terms.art: A beach at high tide and at low tide on two panels.

terms.meaning: High tide is when the sea is at its highest on the shore. Low tide is when it is at its lowest.
terms.example: A fishing boat sits on wet sand at low tide and floats at high tide.
terms.art: A boat on sand and the same boat floating.

terms.meaning: A heap of water raised on the sea by the Moon's pull. The Earth has two bulges at a time, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side.
terms.example: As the Earth turns under the bulges, a coast has two high tides each day.
terms.art: The Earth with two water bulges and the Moon at one side.

terms.meaning: A tide with an extra-high high tide and an extra-low low tide. It comes at new Moon and full Moon.
terms.example: Spring tides have nothing to do with the spring season. The name means 'spring up'.
terms.art: A tide pole showing a big difference between high and low.

terms.meaning: A tide with a small difference between high and low. It comes at the half Moons.
terms.example: At neap tide a beach hardly seems to move.
terms.art: A tide pole showing a small difference between high and low.

terms.meaning: A slow nodding and rocking of the Moon that lets us see a little round its edges, so over time we see more than half of its surface.
terms.example: Because of libration, we can see about 59 out of every 100 parts of the Moon's surface.
terms.art: The Moon seen five times, each tilted slightly differently.

terms.meaning: How much of the light falling on a thing it sends back. The Moon sends back only about 12 parts in every 100.
terms.example: The Moon is about as dark as a tarred road, yet it looks bright against the night.
terms.art: A grey disc with 12 small dots of light bouncing off it out of 100.

terms.meaning: A spacecraft built to touch down gently on another world.
terms.art: A four-legged lander standing on grey ground.

terms.meaning: How wide something looks, measured as a part of the whole sky. The Moon is about half a degree wide, about the width of a small bindi held at arm's length.
terms.example: The Moon is about 110 of its own widths away from us.
terms.art: A hand holding a bindi up at arm's length over the Moon.

explanations.concept: The terminator: where the Moon's day meets its night
explanations.definition: The terminator is the line between the Moon's lit part and its dark part. For a place on the Moon, it is the moment of sunrise or sunset.
explanations.description: The Sun lights half of the Moon at all times. The line between the lit half and the dark half is the terminator, and it moves slowly round the Moon. As the Moon goes through its phases, we see the terminator sweep across its face. On a growing Moon, the terminator is moving over land that is just having its sunrise. On a shrinking Moon, it is crossing land that is having its sunset. For someone standing on the Moon at the terminator, the Sun is low in the sky, just above the horizon. The land there is like the Earth in the first light of morning. The Sun shines almost along the ground, so a long shadow stretches behind every rock. Beyond the terminator is the Moon's night. A place on the near side takes about two weeks to go from sunrise to sunset.
examples: At first quarter, the half Moon, the terminator is a straight line down the middle. The land on it is having its sunrise.
A crescent Moon is mostly terminator, with the Sun low over most of the lit part.
explanations.art: A Moon with a curved terminator line, a mountain near it throwing a long shadow, and a small Sun sketched low over the horizon.

explanations.concept: Long shadows show shape: why half Moons show mountains and full Moons hide them
explanations.definition: We see the shape of rough ground by its shadows. Slanting light makes long shadows and shows every bump. Light from straight behind us makes almost no shadows, and everything looks flat.
explanations.description: A face lit by a torch held under the chin looks full of bumps and hollows. A face lit by a torch held right beside the camera looks flat. The Moon is the same. At full Moon, the Sun is behind us, and the sunlight falls on the Moon from the same direction as we look. We see almost no shadows, so craters and mountains look flat and the Moon looks like a bright, plain disc. At first quarter and last quarter, the Sun lights the Moon from the side. Along the terminator, every crater rim and mountain makes a long shadow, and the tops of peaks catch the light. That is the best time to see the Moon's craters through binoculars. A full Moon is still lovely, and it shows the bright rays from young craters, but it hides shape. Shadows are useful in another way too: you can find the height of a mountain from the length of its shadow.
examples: A farmer's field looks flat at noon but every furrow shows in the low light of early morning. People who search for old buried walls also look for them in the low light of dawn or dusk.
A photographer takes pictures of rock carvings in the early morning or evening, when shadows pick out the carving.
explanations.art: Two Moons side by side. On the left a full Moon looks flat and bright, and on the right a half Moon shows craters with black shadows along its edge.

explanations.concept: What the Moon's face is made of: highlands, seas and craters
explanations.definition: The Moon's face has bright highlands, dark flat plains called maria, and craters everywhere. The craters were made by rocks from space.
explanations.description: The bright parts of the Moon are rough, high ground called highlands. They are thick with craters and are the oldest parts of the surface. The dark patches are huge plains called maria, the Latin word for seas. They are not water. They are lava that flooded out long ago and cooled into dark, flat rock. Craters have a raised rim and sometimes a peak in the middle. They were made when rocks from space hit the surface at very high speed. The Earth was hit too, but wind, rain, rivers and moving ground wore most of its craters away. The Moon has no air and no water, so its craters stay for billions of years. The near side, which is the side we see, has more dark plains than the far side, so the two sides look different. Why the two sides differ is still debated.
examples: The 'hare' that people in India and many other places see in the Moon is made by the dark plains.
Some craters have bright streaks, called rays, spreading out from them. They are splashes of fresh, bright rock from a young crater.
explanations.art: A close-up of the Moon with highlands crowded with craters, a dark flat plain, and a crater cut open to show its rim, floor and central peak.

explanations.concept: The Moon's age and the 29 and a half day month
explanations.definition: The Moon's age is the number of days since the last new Moon. It tells you the phase.
explanations.description: A new Moon has an age of 0. A thin crescent is 2 or 3 days old. A half Moon, the first quarter, is about 7 days old. A full Moon is about 14 or 15 days old. The last quarter is about 22 days old. After about 29 and a half days, the Moon is new again. So if you know the date of the last new Moon, you can work out the age on any day, and from the age you can tell the phase. The Indian calendar does the same with its tithis, which track the Moon's age. Shukla Prathama, the first tithi of the bright half, is near the start, and Ashtami in the bright half falls about when the half Moon shows. Purnima is the full Moon, and Amavasya is the new Moon. Because the month is 29 and a half days long, calendars give months of 29 or 30 days. The actual time between new Moons varies by several hours, so the age is a guide and not exact.
examples: If the new Moon was on the 2nd of the month, the Moon will be a half Moon around the 9th and full around the 16th or 17th.
Hindu festival dates are set by the tithi, which tracks the Moon's age.
explanations.art: A calendar strip showing the days 0 to 29 with a Moon shape under each of the key days, and the words new, first quarter, full and last quarter.

explanations.concept: When does each phase rise and set? A rule you can use
explanations.definition: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. So a rough rule is: multiply the Moon's age in days by 50 minutes. The Moon rises about that long after sunrise, and sets about that long after sunset.
explanations.description: The Moon moves round the Earth in the same direction as the Earth spins, and it covers about 13 degrees a day. The Earth must turn a bit extra each day to catch up, which takes about 50 minutes. This gives a rule of thumb. Multiply the Moon's age in days by 50 minutes. The Moon rises about that long after sunrise. For a Moon aged 7 days, that is 7 times 50 minutes, which is about 6 hours. So a half Moon rises about noon. At sunset the half Moon is high in the sky, and it sets around midnight. A full Moon, aged about 15 days, rises about 12 hours after sunrise, which is near sunset. After that, the Moon rises after dark and is up later each night. The rule is only a guide. The actual gap between moonrises changes from night to night, and it can be as small as about half an hour or as big as over an hour. It also depends on where you live and the season.
examples: A 3-day-old crescent sets about 2 and a half hours after the Sun. You must look soon after sunset.
A 22-day-old half Moon rises at about midnight and is in the sky in the morning.
explanations.art: A clock face with a Sun and a Moon, and a row of Moon shapes showing that each rises about 50 minutes later than the one before.

explanations.concept: The Moon's day: two weeks of sunlight and two weeks of night
explanations.definition: One day and night on the Moon lasts about 29 and a half Earth days. A place near the Moon's equator has about 14 days of sunlight, then about 14 days of night.
explanations.description: The Moon turns once on its axis in about 27 days, and the Sun seems to cross its sky very slowly. A place on the Moon has about two weeks of sunshine and then two weeks of darkness. With no air to hold heat in, the temperature swings are huge. Near the equator, the ground can reach about 120 degrees Celsius at midday and fall to about minus 170 in the night. So a spacecraft that has to work only on solar power may need to finish its work in about 14 days. India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole region on 23 August 2023, when the Sun was just coming up over the site. This gave its lander and rover about one lunar day of sunlight. ISRO reported that they went to sleep as the lunar night began in early September, and that they did not wake up again.
examples: At full Moon, it is lunar noon on the near side. At new Moon, it is lunar midnight there.
A place near the Moon's pole has the Sun low in the sky all day, with long shadows, so some crater floors there never see the Sun.
explanations.art: A lander on grey ground at dawn with long shadows, and a second panel of the same ground at lunar noon with short shadows.

explanations.concept: The same Moon looks different from different places
explanations.definition: Everyone on the night side of the Earth sees the same phase at the same time. But how the Moon is tilted and which side is lit depend on where you stand.
explanations.description: The shape of the Moon's lit part depends on where the Sun is, and that is the same for everyone. The lit side faces the Sun. From India, which is in the northern half of the world, a growing Moon is lit on the right. For people in Australia or South Africa, in the southern half, the Moon looks upside down, so a growing Moon is lit on the left. The tilt also changes with how far north or south you are. Near the equator, a thin crescent is often lit along the bottom, so it looks like a bowl or a boat. Farther from the equator, it leans over. Some calendars, such as the Islamic calendar, start a month when the Moon is first sighted. People look for the first thin crescent low in the western sky after sunset.
examples: Thin crescents in Kochi or Kanyakumari often look like a bowl, and in northern Europe they tend to lean.
A photograph of the half Moon taken in South Africa looks upside down compared with one taken in India.
explanations.art: A thin crescent Moon like a boat in an orange sky over a coconut palm beach, and a leaning crescent over a snowy northern field.

explanations.concept: How big is the Moon and how far away? A bindi will tell you
explanations.definition: The Moon is about 110 of its own widths away from us. Its width is about 3,500 kilometres, and it is about 384,000 kilometres away.
explanations.description: If you hold a small disc at the right distance from your eye, it just covers the Moon. You find that the distance to the disc is about 110 times the disc's width. A bindi 7 millimetres wide has to be about 77 centimetres from your eye. This tells us the Moon is about 110 of its own widths away. If we know the distance to the Moon, we can work out its width. Astronomers found the distance by watching how the Moon shifts against the stars when seen from different places. Today they bounce laser light off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon. The distance is about 384,000 kilometres. Dividing by 110 gives about 3,500 kilometres. That is a little more than the length of India from Kashmir to Kanyakumari, which is about 3,200 kilometres. The Earth is about 12,700 kilometres wide. About 30 Earths would fit in a row between us and the Moon.
examples: Light from the Moon takes about one and a quarter seconds to reach us, much less than the 8 minutes from the Sun.
The Moon's width is about a quarter of the Earth's.
explanations.art: A child with a bindi on a window glass, with a line of sight to a small Moon above the rooftops and a tape measure showing 77 centimetres.

explanations.concept: Tides: the Moon pulls on the oceans
explanations.definition: Tides are the rise and fall of the sea, caused mainly by the Moon's pull on the Earth's water. There are two high tides every day, about 12 and a half hours apart.
explanations.description: The Moon pulls on everything on the Earth, and the pull is stronger on the side nearest the Moon and weaker on the far side. This stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. The Earth turns once a day beneath the two bulges, so a coast sees two high tides and two low tides in a day. The Moon moves on in its orbit while the Earth turns, so the gap between two high tides is about 12 hours and 25 minutes. This means each high tide arrives about 50 minutes later than on the day before, just as moonrise does. Tide times differ from place to place, because of the shape of the coast and the sea floor. The Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat has some of the biggest tides in India. The Sun also pulls on the oceans, with a bit less than half the Moon's effect.
examples: Fishing boats on many coasts of India are launched at high tide and pulled up the beach at low tide.
A tide table in a newspaper or on a phone gives the times for your port.
explanations.art: The Earth with two blue bulges, a Moon at one side, and arrows showing the Earth turning under the bulges.

explanations.concept: Spring tides and neap tides follow the phases
explanations.definition: At new Moon and full Moon the Sun and the Moon pull in a line, and the tides are the biggest, called spring tides. At the half Moons they pull at right angles and the tides are smallest, called neap tides.
explanations.description: At new Moon, the Moon and the Sun are on the same side of the Earth. At full Moon, they are on opposite sides. In both cases the pulls line up and make a bigger bulge. These are spring tides. At the half Moons, the Sun's pull cuts across the Moon's pull and weakens it, so the high tides are not so high and the low tides not so low. These are neap tides. So the tide's size has a rhythm of about two weeks that follows the phases. Fishing families have long watched Amavasya and Purnima for strong tides. You can see this in a tide table: choose a port, write down the height of the day's high tide for a month, and mark the Moon's phase beside it. The highest highs come a day or two after new Moon and full Moon.
examples: At new Moon and full Moon, the seashore is covered and uncovered over a wider strip.
A tidal bore, a wave that rushes up a river as the tide comes in, is strongest at spring tides.
explanations.art: Three small diagrams of the Sun, Earth and Moon: in line at new Moon, at right angles at half Moon, in line again at full Moon, with a tide pole beside each.

explanations.concept: We see more than half of the Moon: libration
explanations.definition: The Moon always shows nearly the same face, but it nods and rocks a little, so over time we see about 59 parts out of every 100 of its surface.
explanations.description: Because the Moon's path is an oval and slightly tilted, the Moon seems to rock from side to side and nod up and down by a few degrees over a month. This is called libration. It lets us peek a little way round the edges. Over a month or a year, astronomers see about 59 percent of the Moon's surface, though never the middle of the far side. Libration also changes the view of craters near the edge. Near the edge a crater looks like a thin oval, and a small libration can turn a crater from hidden to visible. The far side was first photographed in 1959 by the Soviet spacecraft Luna 3.
examples: Each month the same few craters near the edge come and go.
The rocking is slow and small, a few degrees, but it is real and we can see it in photographs taken on different nights.
explanations.art: Five pictures of the Moon, each tilted slightly differently, showing different craters at the edge.

explanations.concept: The Moon is dark but looks bright
explanations.definition: The Moon sends back only about 12 parts in every 100 of the sunlight that falls on it. It looks bright only because the night sky is dark.
explanations.description: The Moon's rocks and dust are grey, as dark as a tarred road. If you could bring a handful of Moon dust into daylight, it would look dark. Yet a full Moon is bright enough to read by, because the sky around it is black. The full Moon is about 400,000 times fainter than the Sun. Still, it is bright enough to make shadows on a clear night. A full Moon is also brighter than you would expect from the size of its lit part, because at full Moon there are no shadows to darken it. A half Moon gives much less than half the light of a full Moon, only about a tenth. Our eyes see the Moon as white because they adjust to the dark and because the colour in its grey rock is faint.
examples: Pictures of the Moon next to a white sheet of paper show it is grey.
A candle looks pale in daylight and bright in the dark, for the same reason.
explanations.art: A grey disc of Moon dust beside a white paper in daylight, and the same Moon bright in a black sky.

explanations.concept: Is there water on the Moon?
explanations.description: The Moon has no seas and no air, but it may have some water. Instruments on India's Chandrayaan-1, launched in 2008, helped to find signs of water in the form of molecules stuck to the surface dust. Some deep craters near the Moon's poles never see sunlight, because the Sun is always low and the crater walls cast shadows. They are among the coldest places known, and ice could last there for billions of years. In 2009 a NASA probe was crashed into one of these craters, and the cloud it threw up contained water. How much there is, and in what form, are still being studied. Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole in 2023 to study the ground there.
examples: Shadows help us see the Moon's mountains. Shadows also keep the ice in the polar craters cold and out of sight.
Water on the Moon would be useful for visiting astronauts and for making rocket fuel.
explanations.art: A dark crater near the Moon's pole with a sunlit rim, a shadowed floor with ice, and a small lander at the edge.

perspectives.explanation: Cold, permanently shadowed craters near the poles may hold ice mixed with the soil, in amounts big enough to be useful. A crash probe, radar and orbiters have each found signs of it.

perspectives.who: A thin layer of water on dust
perspectives.explanation: The solar wind is a stream of tiny particles from the Sun. It may make a very thin layer of water molecules on the dust in sunlit places. The amount is tiny, only traces, and it may come and go with the lunar day.

agreed.text: The Moon's craters were made by rocks from space hitting the surface, not by volcanoes.
agreed.evidence: The craters have raised rims and bright rays. Rocks brought back by the Apollo astronauts had been melted by impacts. Craters made in tests have the same shapes.

agreed.text: The terminator is where the Sun is rising or setting on the Moon, and shadows are longest there.
agreed.evidence: Photographs taken from the Earth and from spacecraft show long shadows along the terminator at every phase, and shorter shadows nearer the full Moon.

agreed.text: The Moon's phase can be worked out from its age, which is the number of days since the last new Moon.
agreed.evidence: Calendars have used a month of about 29 and a half days for thousands of years, and eclipses and new Moons have been predicted correctly from them.

agreed.text: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.
agreed.evidence: Moonrise tables for any city show the same slow shift from night to night, though the exact gap varies.

agreed.text: The Moon's pull on the oceans causes tides, with two high tides a day, and spring tides at new and full Moon.
agreed.evidence: Tide tables from ports around the world match the Moon's position and phase, and they can be predicted years ahead.

agreed.text: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away and about 3,500 kilometres wide.
agreed.evidence: Laser light bounced off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts gives the distance to within a few centimetres. The width follows from the Moon's width in the sky.

agreed.text: A lunar day lasts about 29 and a half Earth days, with about two weeks of sunlight and two weeks of night at most places.
agreed.evidence: Landers have recorded the ground heating up in daylight and freezing in the night, and the Sun's movement across the Moon's sky has been watched from orbit.

challenging.claim: The full Moon is the best night to see the Moon's surface.
challenging.who: Many people, because the full Moon is brightest.
challenging.for: A full Moon is fully lit, so we see the whole face at once and it is very bright.
challenging.against: At full Moon the sunlight comes from behind us, so there are almost no shadows. Craters and mountains look flat. At a half Moon, long shadows along the terminator show them clearly. Galileo noticed this in 1609.

challenging.claim: The Moon's craters are old volcanoes.
challenging.who: Many scientists, up to the early 1900s.
challenging.for: The Moon has dark plains of old lava, and some craters look like volcano mouths.
challenging.against: In 1893 the American geologist Grove Karl Gilbert argued they were made by impacts. Craters are round whichever way the rock arrives, have raised rims and bright rays, and match craters made in tests. Apollo rocks later showed signs of impact. Most scientists accepted the impact idea by the 1960s and 1970s.

challenging.claim: There is one tide bulge, on the side of the Earth facing the Moon.
challenging.for: The Moon pulls the sea towards it, so the sea piles up on the near side.
challenging.against: There are two bulges, one on the near side and one on the far side. That is why there are two high tides a day. The far-side bulge forms because the Moon's pull is weaker there than on the rest of the Earth, so the water there is left behind.

challenging.claim: High tide comes at the same time every day.
challenging.who: Many people, because the Sun rises at nearly the same time each day.
challenging.for: Tides repeat each day, so it seems like the same times should repeat.
challenging.against: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, and the tides follow the Moon. So each high tide comes about 50 minutes later than the day before. A tide table shows the changing times.

challenging.who: Most people and most children's drawings.
challenging.for: The Moon looks white or pale yellow in the night sky.
challenging.against: The Moon is grey and reflects only about 12 parts in every 100 of the light that falls on it, about as dark as a tarred road. It looks white because the sky around it is black.

challenging.claim: There is a lot of water ice on the Moon that we can use.
challenging.who: Some space agencies and companies hope so.
challenging.for: Instruments from India, the United States and others have found signs of water, and some craters near the poles never see the Sun.
challenging.against: How much water there is, where it is and how easy it would be to use are still unknown. This is an active area of study, and the Moon's poles have been visited by only a few spacecraft.

big_questions.q: The brightest Moon shows the least of its own shape. Can you think of other times when more light makes you see less?
big_questions.hint: Think about a face lit from the front and from the side, or a field at noon and at dawn.

big_questions.q: We usually think of a shadow as a dark place where we see nothing. On the Moon, shadows show the shape of the ground. What else do we learn from the dark parts of a picture?
big_questions.hint: Think of a drawing in pencil, a photograph with a dark background, or a silence in music.

big_questions.q: The Moon's lit side always faces the Sun. When you see a crescent in the sky, where is the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Think about the line from the bright edge to the Sun, even if the Sun has set.

big_questions.q: Everyone sees the same phase at the same time, but a child in Australia sees it upside down. Who sees the Moon the right way up?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'up' means, and where the people are standing.

big_questions.q: Chandrayaan-3 was timed to land at lunar dawn and had about two weeks of sunlight. How do people plan their work around something they cannot hurry, like the Moon's slow day?
big_questions.hint: Think of a farmer who plans around the monsoon, or a fisher who plans around the tide.

big_questions.q: The Moon pulls the sea up twice a day without touching it. How can something act on another thing from far away?
big_questions.hint: Think about a magnet, gravity and the way the sea feels the Moon.

big_questions.q: Fishing families have watched Amavasya and Purnima for the biggest tides for hundreds of years, long before there were tide tables. What does it take to learn a pattern like that?
big_questions.hint: Think of how many years a family would need to watch, and how they pass it on.

big_questions.q: People see a hare, a face or an old woman in the Moon's dark patches. If everyone sees something different in the same picture, who is right?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is in the picture and what is added by the viewer.

big_questions.q: Galileo looked through a telescope and reported mountains on the Moon. Some scholars said an invisible clear material must fill the hollows, to keep the Moon smooth. How should we treat an idea that cannot be tested?
big_questions.hint: Think about what test could show the clear material to be there or not.

big_questions.q: Some craters near the Moon's poles have been in shadow for billions of years. What would a place be like if it never saw the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Think about how cold it must be, and what could be kept there.

story.title: The Line Where the Mountains Stand
story.note: Made up. Abirami, her Paati, her classmate Karthik and their flat in Madurai are invented. Real: a full Moon was in the sky on 1 August 2023, a new Moon on 16 August, and India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south polar region on 23 August 2023, a little after six in the evening, at lunar dawn, designed to work for about one lunar day of sunlight. The Moon was nearly a half Moon that evening.
text: Abirami was nine, and she had a problem. The school science fair was in three weeks, and her project was called Mountains on the Moon. She had a pair of binoculars borrowed from her uncle, a drawing book, and a very short time.

On the first night of August, a full Moon rose over the water tank on the roof of the building opposite. It was huge and golden, and every neighbour came up to their terraces to look. Abirami took her binoculars and her drawing book up to the roof, and she held her breath, and she looked.

The Moon was a bright white plate. It had some grey smudges, which her teacher said were old lava plains. But there were no mountains. There were no craters. There was no shadow anywhere. It was as flat and smooth as a thali.
She sat down on the cold floor of the terrace. 'The book is wrong,' she said. 'The Moon is smooth. My project is finished before it started.'

Her Paati was drying chillies on the next terrace. She came over, wiping her hands on her sari, and looked through the binoculars for a long time without saying anything. 'It is a beautiful Moon,' she said finally. 'But it does look as flat as a thali.'
'See?' said Abirami.

Paati sat down next to her. 'I worked for thirty years in the Survey Department,' she said. 'I walked fields with a chain and a staff, from Melur to Usilampatti. I will tell you what we learned. A field at noon looks flat. You can stand in a field with a hill in it, and at noon you will swear it is a table.'
'So what did you do?'

'We started at dawn,' said Paati. 'In the early light, the sun is low and comes in sideways. Every small ridge, every old wall under the soil, every little mound throws a long shadow. The same field, and at sunrise it looks like a map. The hills were always there. The noon light hid them.'
Abirami looked at the Moon again. 'The sun is behind me now,' she said slowly. 'It is shining straight at the Moon. So there are no shadows.'
'Now you are thinking like a surveyor,' said Paati.
'So when will the Moon have sideways light?'

Paati took the almanac off the nail by the door. 'The new Moon is on the sixteenth,' she said, running her finger down the page. 'The Moon is half lit about seven days after new Moon, in the evening. Then the light comes from the side, and the line between the day and night on the Moon is straight down the middle. Along that line, it is sunrise on the Moon. Look there.'
Abirami counted the days on the calendar. It was a long wait. She drew the full Moon in her book anyway, a plain circle, and under it she wrote, 'The wrong night.'

On the twenty-third, the whole school was talking about only one thing. India was going to land a spacecraft on the Moon that evening. Karthik, who sat next to her, said he could not wait. 'They picked the twenty-third on purpose,' said her teacher. 'Can anybody tell me why that day?' Nobody knew. Abirami had a feeling, but she kept it to herself.

At six o'clock, the whole building crowded round Paati's television. When the lander touched down at four minutes past six, Abirami heard the cheering from every floor of the building. Paati wiped her eyes with the end of her sari.
Then Abirami grabbed her binoculars. 'Paati, come up!'

On the terrace, the sky was a pale orange, turning blue. High in the south hung the Moon, almost, but not quite, a half Moon, with its bright side towards the setting Sun. Abirami put the binoculars to her eyes and gasped.

Along the line between the light and the dark, the Moon was not smooth at all. It was crumpled. Craters, big and small, had black crescent shadows inside their rims. Rows of them marched along the edge like footprints. Beyond the line, in the dark part, three tiny bright dots floated by themselves. 'Paati! They are mountain tops!' she said. 'The sun has reached the tops, but not the valleys yet.'
'Just like the hills at Melur,' said Paati.

Abirami drew it all as fast as she could. Then she lowered the binoculars and looked at the bottom of the Moon, near the line. 'The spacecraft is down there,' she said. 'And the Sun has only just come up over it. That is why they chose today. The Sun is low there, and it has two weeks of daylight before it sets. That is how long the machines will work.'
'And then?' asked Paati.
'Then it will be night for two weeks, and very cold,' said Abirami. 'And they will sleep.'

At the science fair, Abirami's poster had a full Moon on one side, bright and flat, and a half Moon on the other, rough with shadows. Across the top she had written: 'Do not look at the bright Moon. Look at the line.' Karthik read it twice. 'I'm going to try that on Saturday,' he said.
story.epiphany: A bright full Moon hides the shape of the Moon's ground, because the light comes straight from behind us. Sideways light along the line between day and night throws long shadows that show mountains and craters.

roots.context: We have looked at the line between the Moon's day and night, at tides and at the Moon's age. Now we ask what the shadows on the Moon teach us about how we see things.

deep_truth.truth: In the Dough Moon experiment, you lit a ball of dough with a torch. With the torch beside your head, the craters nearly vanished. With the torch at the side, they stood out. Light from the side throws shadows, and shadows show shape. So the Moon shows its mountains best along the line between its day and night.
deep_truth.habit: We think the fullest, brightest view is the best view, and that shadows only hide things. On the Moon the brightest night hides the most, and the shadow is what shows the shape.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dough Moon experiment, the torch beside your head showed few craters, and the torch at the side showed many. The same thing happens on the real Moon. At a half Moon, the shadows along the terminator show craters and peaks. At full Moon, there are almost no shadows and the Moon looks flat.

three.who_am_i: What you can see of something depends on where you stand and where the light comes from. So where you are is part of everything you see.
three.what_is_life: Many animals use the Moon to time their lives, and many use shadows to find food. A hunter in dim light may find prey by the shape of a shadow.
three.what_is_this_world: The Moon is a ball of grey rock with mountains and craters. Half of it is always lit by the Sun. How rough it looks to us changes with the angle of the sunlight.

roots.thread: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon keep moving, so the way the Moon is lit keeps changing. On a full Moon night the Moon looks like a flat disc. On a half Moon night the same Moon looks like a land of mountains and craters. The Moon has not changed. Only the angle of the light has. Light and shadow work together here: we need both to see the shape of a thing.

teachings.teaching: Being and not-being give birth to each other. Long and short shape each other. High and low lean on each other.
teachings.link: Light and shadow shape each other on the Moon. Without the shadow, we would not see the mountain, and without the light, we would not see the shadow.

teachings.teaching: Lead me from darkness to light.
teachings.link: On the Moon, the brightest part is not where we see the most. We see the mountains best along the line where dark meets light.

science.text: Craters on the Moon are made by impacts. Slanting light along the terminator shows them best.
We do not yet know how much water ice lies in the Moon's permanently shadowed craters.

other_view.who: Many people who love the full Moon
other_view.view: The full Moon is the most beautiful Moon. Its brightness lights the whole night, and it brings families out to the terrace. Seeing detail is one way to enjoy the Moon, and not the only one. A flat, bright Moon is not a worse Moon, only a different one.

practice.title: Light from the side
practice.say: Hold your hand up. Look at it with a lamp behind your head, then with the lamp at your side. Notice the lines and the bumps on your skin each time. Which light shows more? Breathe in slowly three times as you look. Then think of the line between day and night on the Moon, where the shadows are long.
practice.kid: Hold up your hand. Use a lamp at your side. See the lines and bumps. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: When you have too much light on something, do you see more of it or less?
On the Moon, the shadow shows the mountain. What else do we only understand because of its shadow?
The full Moon is flat and the half Moon is rough. Which one is the real Moon?

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many scholars taught that the Moon and the heavens were perfect, and that the Moon was a smooth, polished ball. The dark patches were explained as stains inside it. In the winter of 1609, Galileo Galilei in Italy pointed a new telescope at the Moon, and he looked at it when it was only partly lit. He saw that the line between light and dark was ragged and not smooth. He saw bright specks in the dark part, which grew and joined the light as the days passed, like mountain tops catching the first sun. He saw round hollows with dark shadows inside their rims. He used the lengths of the shadows to guess how tall the mountains were. He published what he saw in a small book in March 1610. Some scholars said the hollows must be filled with an invisible clear material, to keep the Moon smooth. But nobody could test that, while Galileo's drawings could be checked by anyone who had a telescope.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scholars thought the Moon was a perfectly smooth ball. Galileo showed that the line between its day and night is ragged and that it has mountains and hollows, by looking at the Moon when only part of it was lit.

printables.title: A score sheet with three columns

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. One player is the reader and takes the top card. The back stays hidden.
The reader shows the age on the front. Every other player draws the Moon shape on scrap paper, and writes which side is lit.

Everyone also writes down when the Moon sets or rises, using the rule of thumb. Up to the full Moon, multiply the Moon's age by 50 minutes. The Moon sets about that long after sunset. After the full Moon, multiply the number of days since the full Moon by 50 minutes. The Moon rises about that long after sunset. These times are typical, not exact, and change a little with your city and the season.
The reader reads the back. A right phase is 1 point, a right lit side is 1 point, and a time within an hour is 1 point.
Pass the reader job to the next player after each card.
When the cards run out, the player with the most points wins. If points are equal, the players share the win.

Playing alone? Guess for each card and score yourself. Try to beat your score in a second round. With two to four players, one reader at a time keeps the cards, and the others race to answer on paper.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards (or write the ages and answers on 24 slips of paper) and shuffle them. Find out today's sunset time and write it on a sheet. You will work out the Moon's times from it.
flow.say: Each card tells us the Moon's age. We guess its shape, its lit side and when it sets or rises. First, what time does the Sun set today?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Find today's sunset time.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Read the age, draw the shape, write the lit side and the time. Check the back.

flow.kid: Read one practice card. Draw the Moon. Which side is lit?

check.q: A Moon is 7 days old. About when does it set, if the Sun sets at 6 in the evening?
check.why: Seven times 50 minutes is about 6 hours. Six hours after 6 in the evening is midnight. A 7-day-old Moon is a half Moon and is high in the sky at sunset. Picking 6 in the morning would be right for a full Moon, not a half Moon.

flow.kid: Show a card. Draw the Moon. Write the time. Check the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided question cards: a question about the Moon on the front and the answer on the back

items.f: How long does a day and night on the Moon last?
items.b: About 29 and a half Earth days. That is about two weeks of sunlight and two weeks of night.

items.f: Why does a lander need to land at lunar dawn if it works on sunlight?
items.b: So it has the whole two weeks of daylight to work in before the night comes.

items.f: What is the line between the lit and dark part of the Moon called?
items.b: The terminator.

items.f: At the terminator, is the Sun high or low in the Moon's sky?
items.b: Low, just above the horizon. That is why shadows are long.

items.f: Which phase shows the most craters through binoculars: full or half?
items.b: Half. Light from the side makes long shadows.

items.f: About how hot does the Moon's ground get at midday near the equator?
items.b: About 120 degrees Celsius.

items.f: About how cold does it get in the night near the equator?
items.b: About minus 170 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Why does the Moon get so cold at night?
items.b: There is no air to hold the heat in, so the ground loses heat quickly.

items.f: What are the dark plains on the Moon called?
items.b: Maria, the Latin word for seas. They are old lava, not water.

items.f: How were most of the Moon's craters made?
items.b: By rocks from space hitting the ground.

items.f: Why do craters last so long on the Moon?
items.b: There is no wind, rain or moving ground to wear them away.

items.f: Why can a lander on the Moon not use a parachute?
items.b: There is no air to slow it down.

items.f: About how long does it take light to cross from the Moon to the Earth?
items.b: About one and a quarter seconds.

items.f: Why is a crater near the Moon's pole good for finding ice?
items.b: The floor never sees the Sun, so it stays extremely cold.

items.f: A shadow of a hill on the Moon grows longer. Is the Sun getting higher or lower?
items.b: Lower. Long shadows mean low sun.

items.f: What does a lander use for power in the Moon's day?
items.b: Sunlight, through solar panels.

items.f: What happens to a solar-powered lander in the lunar night?
items.b: It gets no power and gets very cold, so it may sleep and not wake again.

items.f: If the Moon is a half Moon today, about how old is it?
items.b: About 7 days after the new Moon, or about 22 days.

items.f: Why can a rover on the Moon's far side not send signals straight to the Earth?
items.b: The whole Moon is in the way. It needs a relay satellite.

items.f: Is the far side of the Moon always dark?
items.b: No. It gets the same sunlight as the near side, and it is lit at new Moon.

items.f: What is the name of India's lander that landed in 2023?
items.b: Vikram, on Chandrayaan-3.

items.f: When a crater's shadow points left, where is the Sun?
items.b: On the right, the opposite side from the shadow.

items.f: What would you see if you stood on the Moon at lunar noon and looked up?
items.b: A black sky, even though the Sun is shining. There is no air to scatter the light.

items.f: What do we call the Moon's rocks that astronauts and landers study?
items.b: Lunar rocks, or Moon soil. They are grey and dusty.

printables.title: 4 paper rovers and 1 Sun marker to cut out

rules: Each player puts a rover on square 1. Put the Sun marker on step 1 of the day track. Shuffle the question cards.
On your turn, roll the dice and move your rover that many squares. Stop at square 14 if you roll more than you need.
If you land on a QUESTION square, another player reads you the top card. If your answer is right, move forward 1 more square. If it is wrong, stay where you are.
Follow the other squares: a crater sends you back 1, dust makes you miss a turn, a slope sends you back 2, and a sunny ridge sends you forward 2.
When everyone has had a turn, move the Sun marker forward one step. That is one Earth day.
The first rover to reach square 14 wins. If the Sun marker reaches SUNSET at step 14 before anyone has finished, the night wins and everyone's rover freezes.
Playing alone? Try to reach the finish before the Sun marker reaches step 10. If you manage that, play again and try to finish before step 9.
With two to four players, take turns. The Sun marker moves once when everyone has had a turn, so more players do not make the night come sooner.

flow.do: Cut out the board and the 24 question cards, and shuffle the cards. Use a coin, button or bottle cap for each rover and a different small object for the Sun marker. Find one dice from a Ludo or snakes-and-ladders set. If you have none, write 1 to 6 on six paper slips and draw one from a cup. Put every rover on the start.
