flow.parent: Let the children try the questions without help. If they do not know an answer, read the back and move on. The aim is to learn from the cards, not to catch anyone out.
flow.context: In this step, you race along the board and watch the days pass.

flow.do: Check who won, or whether the night won. Talk about why a lander is timed to land at dawn.
flow.say: Did anyone reach the finish? If the night won, what could you change next time? Why did we start at lunar dawn?
flow.kid: Who won? What could a lander do to save time?

check.q: A lander must work in sunlight for as long as possible. When should it land?
check.why: Landing just after sunrise gives about two weeks of daylight. Landing at noon gives only one week, and landing at sunset gives almost none.

flow.think: What else might a spacecraft do to survive the night, other than sleeping?
flow.context: In this last step, you finish the race and talk about timing.

experiments.title: The Dough Moon: which light shows the most craters?
experiments.question: A ball of dough with craters and lumps is lit by a torch from three directions. From which direction can you see the most craters and mountains?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see the most craters when the torch is behind your head, at the side, or behind the dough? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same dough Moon, the same torch, the same distance from the dough and the same seat every time. Make the room equally dark each time. Only the direction of the light changes, so any difference in what you see comes from the light. Count twice: you count once and a helper counts once, because one count can be a fluke. Who does what: with one child and a parent, the child counts and draws while the parent holds the torch. With two to four children, one holds the torch, one writes in the table, and the others each count alone and write their number before they compare. Swap jobs for each light.
results_table: Craters and lumps I counted (out of 9)
Craters and lumps my helper counted

materials.item: a ball of atta dough or clay, about the size of a small orange, pressed on to a plate
things to press craters: the rim of a steel katori, a bottle cap, a marble and your thumb
a bright torch, or a phone torch
a dark room
a ruler
paper and a pencil
a helper to count too
a 50 centimetre piece of string or thread, to keep the torch at the same distance
a few books to rest the torch on, at the height of the plate

experiments.safety: Use an LED torch, which stays cool, and not a bare bulb. Atta dough contains wheat, so if anyone at home has a wheat allergy or gluten problem, use clay or play dough instead and keep it away from their hands and mouth. Do not eat the dough. Keep the marble away from little brothers and sisters. Wash your hands afterwards. Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: A ball of dough with craters and lumps is lit by a torch from three directions. From which direction can you see the most craters and mountains?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the dough Moon three times, once for each light, and shade the shadows you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a model Moon from dough and light it from three directions. You find out which light shows craters and mountains best.

setup.art: A ball of dough on a plate with six round craters pressed in and three lumps pinched up, beside a katori, a marble and a bottle cap.
setup.caption: 1. Press six craters and pinch three lumps into the dough Moon.

setup.art: A child seated 50 centimetres from the plate, with a torch held right beside her head and shining on the dough, in a dark room.
setup.caption: 2. Light 1, full Moon: hold the torch beside your head, 50 centimetres from the dough, and shine it at the dough.

setup.art: The same dough Moon with the torch on a stand at the side, low and shining across the dough, and long shadows inside the craters.
setup.caption: 3. Light 2, half Moon: put the torch at the side, low, shining across the dough.

flow.do: Show your child the dough, the torch and the tools. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will make a dough Moon and light it from three places. Beside your head is like a full Moon. At the side is like a half Moon. Where will we see the most craters? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Where will you see the most craters? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which light do you think will show the most craters?
good: Beside my head, because it lights the whole thing.
At the side, because of shadows.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess the torch beside the head, because it is the brightest. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dough Moon test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Pinch the dough into a ball on a plate. 2. Press three big craters and three small ones with the katori, the cap, the marble and your thumb. 3. Pinch up three lumps for mountains. 4. Make the craters deep and the lumps tall.
flow.say: Press craters in the dough with the katori and cap. Make some big and some small. Pinch up three lumps for mountains. We now have nine things to count.
flow.kid: Make six craters. Pinch three lumps. That makes nine things.
flow.parent: Deep craters with sharp rims show up best. A shallow dent will not make a clear shadow. If the dough is sticky, dust it with a little flour. Keep the plate in the same place for all three tests.

check.q: Why do we make craters of different sizes, and some deep?
options: So there are different things to count and the shadows are clear
check.why: A mix of big and small, deep and shallow craters gives us a real test of what each light shows. Deep craters make clear shadows. Using up the dough is just a side effect.

flow.context: In this step, you build the dough Moon with six craters and three lumps.

flow.do: 1. Sit 50 centimetres from the plate. Use the string to check. 2. Make the room dark: do this at night with curtains closed, since a phone torch looks weak in daylight. 3. Hold the torch beside your head, 50 centimetres from the dough (the string stretched from the dough to the torch), and shine it at the dough. 4. Count the craters and lumps you can see. 5. Ask the helper to count too. 6. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Hold the torch beside your head, like the Sun behind us at full Moon. Count the craters and lumps you can see. Is it hard? Draw it.
flow.kid: Hold the torch by your head. Count the craters. Draw the dough.

ask.q: How many craters and lumps can you see, and what do they look like?
good: I can see circles but no shadows.

flow.parent: With the torch beside the head, the shadows fall behind the craters, where you cannot see them. You may count only 3 or 4 of the 9 things. The dough will look bright, flat and pale. That is the full Moon view. Write the numbers exactly as you counted them. The exact counts differ with your dough and torch. Do not worry if the torch beside the head shows 4 or 5, as long as it shows clearly fewer than the torch at the side does in the next step. If it does not, press the craters deeper, make the room darker, or move the torch further round to the side in the next step.
flow.context: In this step, you light the dough Moon from behind your head, like a full Moon.

flow.do: 1. Move the torch to the side of the plate. Keep it 50 centimetres away (use the string). Rest it low on the books, so its light skims across the dough. 2. Keep your seat the same. 3. Count what you see. 4. Ask the helper to count. 5. Measure the shadow of the tallest lump with the ruler.
flow.say: Now move the torch to the side, low. This is like the half Moon. Count again. What has changed? Measure the longest shadow.
flow.kid: Move the torch to the side. Count again. Measure a shadow.

ask.q: What changed when the light came from the side?

flow.parent: You should count most or all of the 9 things, with dark crescent shadows inside the craters and long shadows beside the lumps. If you do not, press the craters deeper and try again. Keep the torch low and at the dough's height. A shadow of a few centimetres is normal.

check.q: Why do you see more craters with the light from the side?
options: The side light makes long shadows inside the craters
check.why: Light from the side skims across the dough and makes shadows. The shadows show the shape of each crater and lump. Picking 'brighter' is a common guess, but the torch is the same.

flow.context: In this step, you light the dough Moon from the side, like a half Moon.

flow.do: 1. Move the torch behind the plate, a little to one side. Keep it 50 centimetres from the dough, so the light grazes the dough's back edge. 2. Count what you see. 3. Switch off the torch.
flow.say: Last, put the torch behind the dough, a little to the side. This is like a crescent Moon. How much can you see now?
flow.kid: Put the torch behind the dough. Count again.
flow.parent: Only a thin edge of the dough is lit, and the front is mostly dark. You may count 2 to 5 things. The lit edge shows long shadows.
flow.context: In this step, you light the dough Moon from behind, like a crescent.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the best light for seeing craters comes from the side. What I saw: I counted 3 with the torch by my head, 9 with the torch at the side. Why: light from the side makes long shadows, and shadows show shape. On the real Moon, the sideways light along the terminator makes shadows, so a half Moon shows mountains best.
flow.think: At full Moon the Sun shines straight on to the Moon from behind us. What would you see if you stood on the Moon at that moment?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found and link it to the Moon.

experiments.title: Moonrise Detective: how much later does the Moon rise each night?
experiments.question: People say the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Is that true for your city, and is the gap the same every night?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many minutes later will the Moon rise each night? Will the gap be the same every night? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same city and the same source for all ten days, and write every time on the 24-hour clock. Use ten nights in a row. Start two days after a new Moon, so the times do not jump over midnight. Only the date changes, so any change in the time comes from the Moon's movement.
results_table: Minutes later than the day before

materials.item: a phone, a weather app or a newspaper that gives moonrise times
the date of the last new Moon, from a calendar or panchang
a notebook with squared paper
a ruler and a pencil
a calculator, if you like

experiments.safety: A grown-up should help with the phone. Do not stand near the edge of a roof to look for the Moon.

schedule.what: People say the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Is that true for your city, and is the gap the same every night?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a line graph with the day on the bottom and the moonrise time up the side. Write the average gap in minutes. Write your day 11 guess and the real time, and the difference in minutes.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you collect ten days of moonrise times for your city and work out the gap from day to day. You test the rule that the Moon rises about 50 minutes later.

setup.art: A phone showing a table of moonrise times for ten days in a row, next to a notebook with a table drawn in it.
setup.caption: 1. Find ten days of moonrise times for your city and copy them into a table.

setup.art: A notebook with a subtraction written beside each row giving the gap in minutes, and a calculator.
setup.caption: 2. Work out how many minutes later the Moon rose each day.

setup.art: A line graph with ten dots going up gently from left to right, and a ruler laid along the dots.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a graph of the moonrise times.

flow.do: Show your child the notebook. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will collect ten days of moonrise times for our city. How many minutes later will the Moon rise each day? Will the gap be the same every day? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. How much later does the Moon rise each day? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the Moon rises later each day?
good: It is moving round the Earth.
It is slower than the Sun.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children guess 24 hours or one hour. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Moonrise Detective. You guess before you look at the data.

flow.do: 1. Find the date of the last new Moon. 2. Start two days after it. 3. Use a weather app or newspaper to find the moonrise time for your city on ten days in a row. 4. Copy the times into the table on a 24-hour clock. 5. Write the Moon's age beside each day.
flow.say: Find the last new Moon. Start two days after it. Look up the moonrise time for ten days in a row. Copy each into the table. Use a 24-hour clock, so 4 in the afternoon is 16:00.
flow.kid: Find ten days of moonrise times. Copy them into the table.
flow.parent: Weather apps and sites such as the time and date website list moonrise by city. A panchang or wall calendar may give moonrise as chandrodaya. If you cannot find ten days, use as many as you can, at least six. Starting two days after a new Moon means the moonrise times run from morning to evening without jumping past midnight. For one child, the parent finds the table and the child copies it. For two to four children, each child can look up a different city (for example Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and your own), then compare the average gaps at the end. No special materials are needed. If you can, step outside on one of the days at the moonrise time and see the Moon yourself.

check.q: Why do we start two days after a new Moon?
options: So the times keep going up without jumping across midnight
Because the Moon cannot be seen before
check.why: At a new Moon, the Moon rises near sunrise. Ten days later it rises in the afternoon. Over those days the time gets steadily later, with no jump. Later in the month, moonrise passes midnight and the clock numbers start again from zero. Picking 'cannot be seen' mixes up rising with being easy to see.

flow.context: In this step, you collect the data you need.

flow.do: 1. For each day, subtract the time of the day before. 2. Write the gap in minutes. 3. Add up all the gaps and divide by the number of gaps to find the average.
flow.say: Subtract each day's time from the next. For example, 10:40 take away 09:46 is 54 minutes. Write the gap. Then find the average.
flow.kid: Find the gap between each day and the day before. Find the average.

ask.q: Is the gap the same every day?
good: It is sometimes more and sometimes less.

flow.parent: Expect an average near 50 minutes, but single gaps may be anywhere from about 30 to about 70 minutes, depending on your city and the time of year. Do not worry if your gaps are not all the same. That is a real result. For subtracting times: 10:40 less 09:46 is 54 minutes.

check.q: The gaps in your table are 48, 52, 55, 50 and 45 minutes. What is the average?
check.why: Add them up to get 250, then divide by 5. The average is 50 minutes. 250 is the total and not the average.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the gaps and their average.

flow.do: Draw a graph on squared paper. Put the days along the bottom and the moonrise times up the side. Mark a dot for each day. Lay a ruler along the dots. Then use your average gap to predict the moonrise on day 11, write it down, and only afterwards look it up. How far off were you?
flow.say: Draw a dot for each day on the graph. Lay a ruler along the dots. Do they make a straight line? Which way does it slope? Now guess day 11 from your average, before you look it up.
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each day. Lay a ruler along them. Is it straight?

ask.q: What does the slope of the line tell you?
good: The Moon rises later each day.
The gap is about the same every day.

flow.parent: The dots should rise roughly in a straight line sloping upwards. Some dots may sit a little above or below the line. That is normal.
flow.context: In this step, you draw a graph of the moonrise times.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see in the data? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, but not exactly. What I saw: the average gap was 51 minutes, and single gaps ran from 45 to 55. Why: the Moon moves round the Earth in the same direction as the Earth spins, so the Earth must turn a little extra each day to catch up. The Moon's speed and the angle of its path change slightly, so the gap changes a little.
flow.think: Use your average to guess when the Moon will rise 20 days after the last new Moon. Why will your guess not be exact?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found.

experiments.title: The Bindi Moon: how many Moon-widths away is the Moon?
experiments.question: How far away is the Moon, measured in its own width? Can a small bindi on a window glass cover the whole Moon?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How far from your eye must a small bindi be to cover the Moon exactly? Will it be a few centimetres, or a few metres? How many times its own width? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bindi, the same window and the same Moon each time. Close the same eye and look from the same height. Measure the distance three times and use the average, because one measurement can be a fluke. Only your position changes, so any difference comes from where you stood. With several children, each child lines up the bindi on their own and measures. If everyone gets a ratio close to 110, your result is more trustworthy.
results_table: Distance from bindi to my eye (mm)

materials.item: a round bindi or a round sticker, between 5 and 8 millimetres wide (a packet of bindis costs about Rs 10), stuck on a window glass or on a clear polythene sheet taped to a stick
a long tape measure, or a string and a ruler
a window or an open balcony with a clear view of the Moon, with the room lights off so the glass does not show reflections
a helper to hold the string (with 2 to 4 children, one aligns, one holds the string, one writes)
a calculator

experiments.safety: Use this only for the Moon. Never try it on the Sun, and never look at the Sun. Stand safely at the window, away from a balcony edge. A grown-up should help near high windows.

schedule.what: How far away is the Moon, measured in its own width? Can a small bindi on a window glass cover the whole Moon?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bindi, your eye and the Moon in a line, and label the two distances.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find the distance at which a small bindi on a window covers the Moon. You work out how many Moon-widths away the Moon is, and how wide the Moon is.

setup.art: A bindi stuck on a window glass with the Moon showing beyond it, and a child standing back with one eye closed.
setup.caption: 1. Stick the bindi on the glass. Stand back and close one eye.

setup.art: A child with a string held from her eye to the bindi by a helper, and a ruler against the string.
setup.caption: 2. Move until the bindi just covers the Moon. Measure from your eye to the bindi.

flow.do: Show your child the bindi and the window. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will stick a bindi on the window. When we stand back, the bindi can cover the whole Moon. How far back must we stand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. How far back for the bindi to cover the Moon? Why?

ask.q: Will you stand close to the glass or far from it?
good: Close, because the Moon is small.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Pick a night when the Moon is easy to see. Use a night between about 9 and 17 days after new Moon, when the whole round Moon is lit, so the bindi can cover all of it. On a half Moon, cover the straight edge, which is as long as the Moon is wide. A thin crescent does not work, because you cannot see its full width. The Moon should be at least a little way above the horizon so the window glass does not tilt the view.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bindi Moon. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: 1. Measure the bindi's width in millimetres with a ruler. 2. Stick it on the window glass, at the height of your eye. 3. Write the width in the table.
flow.say: Measure how wide the bindi is. Write the number. Stick it on the window at the height of your eye.
flow.kid: Measure the bindi. Stick it on the window glass.
flow.parent: A 7 millimetre bindi is ideal. A smaller bindi needs you to stand closer, and a bigger one means standing far back. If the bindi is a different shape, use its widest part.

check.q: Why do we write down the bindi's width before measuring anything else?
options: We will need it for the sum later
check.why: The ratio of distance to width is the answer, so we need both numbers. Making the table longer is not a reason.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the bindi and put it on the window.

flow.do: 1. Close one eye. 2. Stand back and move your head until the bindi exactly covers the Moon. 3. Hold still. 4. Ask your helper to hold a string from the bindi to your open eye. 5. Measure the string in millimetres. 6. Do it three times.
flow.say: Close one eye. Move back and forth until the bindi exactly hides the Moon. Hold still. Your helper measures from the bindi to your eye. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Close one eye. Move until the bindi hides the Moon. Measure.

ask.q: What did you notice about the distance?
good: It was bigger than I thought.
It was about the same each time.
The Moon is very far away.

flow.parent: Use only one eye, or your two eyes will see the bindi in two places. Your three measurements may differ by a few centimetres. That is normal. For a 7 millimetre bindi, expect about 75 to 85 centimetres (typical, not exact). If the Moon moves out from behind the bindi, line it up and measure again. If the window does not face the Moon, use an open balcony and let the helper hold the clear polythene with the bindi on it at the same height as your eye. If clouds hide the Moon or you cannot find it, try another night.

check.q: Why do we close one eye?
options: Two eyes see the bindi in two places
check.why: Each eye sees from a slightly different place, so with two eyes the bindi lines up with the Moon in different positions. One eye gives a single line of sight. Picking 'the Moon is too bright' mixes up a side effect with the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you find where the bindi covers the Moon and measure the distance.

flow.do: 1. Divide each distance by the bindi's width. 2. Find the average of your three answers. 3. The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away. Divide 384,000 by your average. 4. Compare the answer with the length of India, about 3,200 kilometres.
flow.say: Divide the distance by the bindi's width. This tells us how many bindi-widths away the Moon is. Then divide 384,000 kilometres by that. What do you get?
flow.kid: Divide the distance by the width. Find the average. Work out the Moon's width.

ask.q: How wide is the Moon, and how does it compare with India?
good: A bit wider than India is long.

flow.parent: You should get a ratio near 110 (typical), with a range of about 100 to 120. A 7 millimetre bindi at 77 centimetres gives 770 divided by 7, which is 110. Then 384,000 divided by 110 is about 3,490 kilometres. The real width is about 3,474 kilometres. Do not worry if you get a number between 3,200 and 3,800.

check.q: The bindi is 7 millimetres wide and is 770 millimetres from your eye. What is the ratio?
check.why: 770 divided by 7 is 110. So the Moon is about 110 of its own widths away. Picking 77 uses the distance in centimetres.

flow.context: In this step, you work out how wide the Moon is.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you measure? Why does a small bindi cover a big Moon?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Moon is about 110 of its own widths away. What I saw: a 7 millimetre bindi covered the Moon at about 77 centimetres, so the ratio was about 110. Why: a small thing close to the eye can cover a big thing far away if they are in the same proportion. The same works for the Sun, which is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times further away.
flow.think: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. What does that tell you about how far away it is?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found.

activities.title: Torch on a Coin: where does the shadow fall?

materials.item: a stack of five coins, or a small eraser, standing on the paper
a sheet of white paper
a torch
a ruler
a few books to rest the torch on

activities.safety: Use an LED torch. Do not shine it into anyone's eyes. Keep the coins away from little ones.

schedule.what: Torch on a Coin: where does the shadow fall?

activities.record: Draw the stack and its shadow three times: torch above, torch halfway up, torch low at the side. Write the shadow length from the ruler each time, and which light showed the shape best.
activities.context: This is a quick first activity. You light a stack of coins with a torch from different directions and notice what the shadows do.

setup.art: A coin lying on white paper with a torch directly above it, and almost no shadow.
setup.caption: 1. Light the coin from straight above. Notice the shadow.

setup.art: The same coin with the torch low at the side, and a long shadow stretching across the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Light the coin from the side, low. Notice the shadow.

flow.do: Stand the stack of coins on the paper. Make the room dim. Hold the torch right above it, then halfway up (about 45 degrees), then low at the side, always about 30 centimetres away. Each time, measure the length of the shadow with the ruler and write it down.
flow.say: Look at the coins with the torch above. Now halfway. Now low at the side. Measure the shadow each time. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Light the coin from above. Then from the side. What changes?

ask.q: What happened to the shadow when the torch moved to the side?
good: I could see the shape of the coin.

flow.parent: From straight above, the shadow is a thin ring or nothing. From the side, it stretches. Expect about 0 centimetres from above, and a few centimetres from the side. Do not explain yet. Ask what your child notices and wonders. For 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch, one measures and one records, then swap.
flow.context: This is a quick start. You notice how the direction of light changes a shadow before anyone explains it.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you which light shows the coin's thickness better, and to draw it. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Which light shows that the coin has a thickness? Draw the coin with each light. Here is a puzzle. The Sun's light comes from behind us at full Moon. What might that do to the Moon's craters?
flow.kid: Which light shows the coin's thickness? Draw both.

check.q: Which light makes a bump show up best?
options: Light from the side, at a low angle
Light from straight behind the viewer
check.why: Light from a low angle makes long shadows, and the shadows show the bump. Light from behind the viewer makes almost none, so the bump looks flat.

flow.think: If a mountain makes a long shadow when the Sun is low, what will its shadow be like at midday?
flow.context: In this step, you decide which light shows shape and meet the puzzle of this unit.

activities.title: Catch Up: why the Moon's month is longer than one trip round

materials.item: a lamp or torch to be the Sun
an orange or a ball to be the Earth
a small ball or lime to be the Moon
a big sheet of paper (a newspaper page is fine) with a circle about 30 centimetres wide drawn on it, for the Earth's path round the Sun
2 long pencils to be pointers
a ruler or a few books to hold the lamp up so it shines across the table

activities.safety: Use a torch or an LED lamp, which stays cool. Do not touch a hot bulb.

schedule.what: Catch Up: why the Moon's month is longer than one trip round

activities.record: Draw the Sun, the Earth in two places on its path and the Moon. Mark how much further the Moon had to move to be new again.
activities.context: In this activity, you model why the Moon takes about 29 and a half days from new Moon to new Moon, but only about 27 days to go once round the Earth.

setup.art: A table with a lamp at one end, a paper circle for the Earth's path, an orange on the circle and a small ball between the orange and the lamp.
setup.caption: 1. Put the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in a line, with the Moon between them. This is a new Moon.

setup.art: The orange moved a short way along the paper circle, the small ball taken round it once, and a pencil pointing from the orange to the faraway star.
setup.caption: 2. Move the Earth a little along its path. Take the Moon once round it.

setup.art: The small ball not yet between the orange and the lamp, with an arrow showing how much further it must go.
setup.caption: 3. Look: the Moon is not yet new. It must go a little further.

flow.do: 1. Put the lamp at one end of the table. 2. Put the paper circle in the middle. 3. Put the orange on the circle, on the side nearest the lamp. 4. Put the small ball between the orange and the lamp. 5. Lay pencil A on the table, pointing from the orange across the small ball towards the lamp. 6. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: This is a new Moon. The Moon is between the Earth and the Sun. Now the Moon goes once round the Earth. When it has gone all the way round, will it be a new Moon again? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The Moon goes round once. Will it be new again? Why?

ask.q: When the Moon has gone once round the Earth, will it be exactly in line with the Sun again?
good: Yes, it has gone all the way round.
No, the Earth has moved on.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say yes. The point of the activity is that the Earth moves along its own path while the Moon goes round. For 2 to 4 children, one moves the Earth, one moves the Moon, one holds the pencils and one records. With one child, the parent can hold the lamp. The model is small, so it is the idea that matters, not the exact angles.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch Up. You guess before you move anything.

flow.do: 1. Move the orange a short way along its paper circle, about one twelfth of the way round. 2. Lay pencil B beside the orange, parallel to pencil A, so it points the same way as before. 3. Take the small ball once round the orange until it lies along pencil B again. 4. Look at where the lamp is now.
flow.say: Move the Earth a little along its path. Lay the second pencil parallel to the first. Take the Moon once round, until it lies along the second pencil. Where is the lamp now? Is the Moon between the Earth and the lamp?
flow.kid: Move the Earth along. Take the Moon round once. Is it new?

ask.q: Is the Moon between the Earth and the Sun now?
good: It has to go a little further.

flow.parent: After one trip round, the Moon points the same way as before, as if towards the same far-off star. But the Earth has moved, so the lamp is in a different direction. The Moon has not quite reached the line between the Earth and the lamp. On the real Moon, covering that last bit takes about two more days. One twelfth of the way round is how far the Earth moves in about a month.

check.q: Why is the Moon not new yet after one trip round?
options: The Earth has moved, so the Sun is in a new direction
check.why: The Earth goes round the Sun at the same time as the Moon goes round the Earth. After a month, the line to the Sun has turned. The Moon needs about two more days to catch up. The lamp, like the Sun, has not moved.

flow.context: In this step, you move the Earth and take the Moon once round.

flow.do: Take the small ball a little further round until it is between the orange and the lamp again. Estimate how much further it had to go, as a fraction of one trip round.
flow.say: Now take the Moon a little further, until it is between the Earth and the lamp. This is a new Moon. About how much extra did it need?
flow.kid: Move the Moon a bit further. Now it is new. How much extra?

ask.q: How much further than one trip did the Moon need to go?
good: About a twelfth of a circle.

flow.parent: The extra is about one twelfth of a trip, which at 27 days a trip is about two days. So the time from new Moon to new Moon is about 27 plus 2, which is about 29 and a half days.
flow.context: In this step, you take the Moon on to the next new Moon.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why is the month longer than one trip round?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Moon needs extra time to line up with the Sun. What I saw: after one trip, the Moon was not between the Earth and the Sun. Why: the Earth moved along its path round the Sun, so the Sun was in a new direction.
flow.think: If the Earth went round the Sun more slowly, would the month be longer or shorter?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found.

activities.title: Tide Detective: do the biggest tides come at new and full Moon?

materials.item: a phone, a newspaper or a website with a tide table for a port, for 15 days. Chennai, Mumbai, Kochi or Visakhapatnam all have one
a Moon calendar or panchang to show the phase on each day
squared paper
coloured pencils

activities.safety: A grown-up should help with the phone or computer.

schedule.what: Tide Detective: do the biggest tides come at new and full Moon?

activities.record: Draw a bar chart of the height of the day's highest tide for 15 days. Colour the bars on new Moon and full Moon days in one colour and the half Moon days in another.
activities.context: In this activity, you read a real tide table and a Moon calendar, and look for a pattern between the Moon's phase and the size of the tides.

setup.art: A phone showing a tide table with times and heights, next to a notebook with a table for fifteen days.
setup.caption: 1. Find a tide table for fifteen days and copy the highest tide each day.

setup.art: A bar chart of fifteen bars with tall bars at the two ends and the middle coloured differently, and a Moon calendar beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the bars and mark the Moon's phase beneath each day.

flow.do: Tell your child what a tide table is. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: A tide table lists when the sea is high and low, and how high. When in the month will the tides be biggest? At new Moon, at half Moon or at full Moon? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. When are the tides biggest? Why?

ask.q: Which Moon do you think gives the biggest tides?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say only the full Moon.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tide Detective. You guess before you look at the data.

flow.do: 1. Find a tide table for a port. 2. Write the height of the highest tide on each of 15 days in a row. 3. Find the Moon's phase for each day on a calendar. 4. Draw the bar chart.
flow.say: Look up the tide table. For each of fifteen days, write down the highest tide, in metres. Then find out the Moon's phase for each day.
flow.kid: Find the tide table. Write the highest tide each day. Add the Moon's phase.
flow.parent: Use a port you can find a table for. Inland families can choose any port. If there is no table to hand, a grown-up can search for the port's name and 'tide table'. The tide range for Indian ports is often 1 to 3 metres, and larger in Gujarat. If you cannot find a table, you can use the made-up practice numbers 1.2, 1.4, 1.7, 2.0, 2.1, 1.9, 1.6, 1.3, 1.2, 1.4, 1.7, 2.0, 2.1, 1.9 and 1.6 metres. Choose a start day about 3 days before a new Moon or full Moon, so that 15 days cover two of them. For 2 to 4 children, each child can take a different port and compare charts. If you use the made-up numbers, treat day 3 as the new Moon and day 10 as the full Moon. They are practice numbers, not real tides. If your port has a small tide range, the pattern still shows but the bars differ less.
flow.context: In this step, you collect fifteen days of tide heights and Moon phases.

flow.do: 1. Look at the bars. Find the days with the tallest bars. 2. Look at the Moon's phase on those days. 3. Look at the days with the shortest bars. 4. Write what you notice.
flow.say: Which days have the tallest bars? What was the Moon's phase on those days? And on the days with the shortest bars?
flow.kid: Find the tallest bars. What was the Moon like? And the shortest?

ask.q: What pattern did you find between the tides and the Moon?
good: The tallest bars come a day or two after new Moon and full Moon.
The shortest bars come at the half Moons.

flow.parent: You should find the biggest tides a day or two after the new Moon and full Moon, and the smallest tides near the half Moons. The pattern comes back about every two weeks. The effect is clearest if you cover at least two weeks. Local weather can disturb it.

check.q: In your data, the biggest tides come at new Moon and full Moon. What does that tell you?
options: When the Sun and Moon pull in a line, tides are bigger
The sea is bigger at night
check.why: At new Moon and full Moon, the Sun and the Moon pull along the same line, so their pulls add up. At the half Moons they pull across each other, and the tides are smaller. Picking 'at night' mixes up the time of day with the phase.

flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern between tides and the Moon.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see in the table? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the biggest tides come at new and full Moon. What I saw: the tallest bars were a day or two after those Moons. Why: the Sun and the Moon pull along one line, so their pulls add up. Fishing families have long watched Amavasya and Purnima for this reason.
flow.think: Why might a tide table be useful to a fisherman, a ship's captain and a child collecting shells?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found.

projects.title: The Terminator Log: five evenings of the growing Moon

materials.item: binoculars, if you can borrow a pair (optional, see the shopping list), or a phone with a zoom camera
a drawing notebook and a pencil
a window, balcony or terrace with a clear view of the western sky
a clock

projects.safety: Use binoculars only after the Sun has set well below the horizon. Never point binoculars at the Sun, not even at sunset. A grown-up should come with you to a roof or a balcony, and stay away from the edge.

schedule.what: Evening 1: draw the thin crescent and mark the line between light and dark.
Evening 2: draw the Moon and compare.
Evening 3: look along the line between light and dark with binoculars.
Evening 4: draw craters and their shadows.
Evening 5: draw, then lay out all five and compare.

projects.record: Draw the Moon's lit shape on each evening, and mark the line between light and dark. Note any dark patches or craters near the line. At the end, write which craters were on the line on which nights.
projects.context: In this project, you draw the growing Moon on five evenings and watch the line between day and night move. You see how the same craters light up in turn.

setup.art: A child on a balcony at dusk, holding binoculars and looking at a thin crescent Moon in the western sky.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the Moon at the same time each evening, after sunset.

setup.art: Five drawn Moons in a row from a thin crescent to a half Moon, with a dotted line marking the edge of the light on each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the lit shape and mark the line between light and dark.

flow.do: On the first evening, about three days after a new Moon, look for the thin crescent in the west soon after sunset. Draw its shape. Mark the line between light and dark. Write the date and the time.
flow.say: Find the thin Moon in the west after sunset. Draw its shape. Draw a dotted line along the edge of the light. Write the date and time.
flow.kid: Find the Moon after sunset. Draw it. Mark the edge of the light.

ask.q: Where is the line between light and dark on the Moon?
good: It's the curved line away from the Sun.

flow.parent: Choose a time 30 to 45 minutes after sunset, and use that same time each evening. Use the naked eye first, then binoculars. If you see a dark oval patch near the edge, that is one of the Moon's dark plains. Do not worry about names. If the western sky is blocked by buildings, begin on evening 2 or 3 instead, when the Moon is higher. Without binoculars you can still see the line and the dark plains, but not craters, so draw the line and the plains. If cloud hides the Moon one night, it does not matter. Use any 5 clear evenings in the first 10 days after new Moon, and write the Moon's age beside each drawing. You can also look at NASA's Moon pictures for the date you missed. In the monsoon, you may need to wait for the next month.
flow.context: This is evening 1 of the Terminator Log. You draw the Moon's first shape.

flow.do: On the second evening, draw the Moon again at the same time. Mark the line between light and dark. Compare it with yesterday.
flow.say: Draw the Moon again. Is more of it lit tonight? Where has the line moved?
flow.kid: Draw the Moon again. Where has the line moved?
flow.parent: The lit part grows each night, and the line moves away from the bright edge. Keep drawings the same size, about 8 centimetres wide.
flow.context: This is evening 2 of the Terminator Log. You draw the Moon again and compare it with yesterday.

flow.do: On evenings 3 and 4, draw the Moon again. Use binoculars to look along the line between light and dark. Draw any craters you can see and their shadows.
flow.say: Look through binoculars along the line. Can you see craters? Which side are the shadows on? Draw them.
flow.kid: Look along the line. Draw the craters. Draw the shadows.

ask.q: Which side of a crater is the shadow on?
good: The side away from the Sun.

flow.parent: Brace your elbows on the railing, and hold the binoculars steady. Craters along the line have dark crescent shadows. Beyond the line, you may see tiny bright dots, which are mountain tops catching sunlight before the valleys. With 2 to 4 children, give each child a notebook and pass the binoculars every minute or so.

check.q: A crater's shadow lies on the side away from the Sun. Where would the Sun be if the shadow points to the left?
check.why: A shadow always points away from the light. If it points left, the light comes from the right. A growing Moon is lit from the right when seen from India.

flow.wait: Leave it for two evenings, and look once each evening
flow.context: These are evenings 3 and 4 of the Terminator Log. You look for craters along the line.

flow.do: On evening 5, draw the Moon for the last time. Lay your five drawings side by side. Look at how the line moved, and which craters were on the line each night.
flow.say: Lay your drawings in a row. How did the line between light and dark move? Which craters were on the line on which night?
flow.kid: Lay out your five drawings. How did the line move?

ask.q: Which night showed the most craters?
good: The nights when the line crossed the middle of the Moon.

flow.parent: The line moves across the Moon over the days, lighting up new land at the sunrise edge. Each night different craters sit on the line. The half Moon night usually shows the most craters because the line runs through the middle of the face.

check.q: Why does a crater look best when it is on the line between light and dark?
options: The Sun is low there, so its shadows are long
It is nearest to the Earth
check.why: On the line, the Sun has only just risen over that land, so it is low and the shadows are long. A crater far from the line has the Sun high above it and short shadows.

flow.context: This is evening 5 of the Terminator Log. You compare all five drawings.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see in your drawings? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the best place to see craters is along the line between light and dark. What I saw: craters on the line had dark shadows, and the line moved across the Moon each night. Why: on the line the Sun is low and the shadows are long.
flow.think: Where will the line between light and dark be at the full Moon?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what your drawings showed.

challenges.title: Land at Lunar Dawn: pick the best day for a landing
challenges.problem: A small lander uses only sunlight and works for about 14 days. Pick the best day to land it at the centre of the Moon's near side, in a month when the new Moon is on the 4th. Say when its sunrise, noon and sunset will be, and what the Moon will look like from India on each of those days.
constraints: Use only the Moon calendar. The new Moon is on the 4th, and the month has 30 days.
The Sun rises at the centre of the near side at the first quarter, shines overhead at the full Moon, and sets at the last quarter.
The lander needs about one day after sunrise to warm up.
It must finish its work before the Sun sets.
materials: a ball and a torch, if you want to test your idea
general: Count 7 days from the new Moon for the first quarter, 14 or 15 days for the full Moon and 22 days for the last quarter.
Pick the day just after sunrise, so the lander has the whole day to work.
Draw a small calendar with the phases and mark the three days.
creative: Choose a site near the Moon's pole, where the Sun stays low and some crater rims are lit for most of the year. Say what the advantages and risks are.
Add a heater and a battery so the lander can survive part of the night. Say what you gain and lose.
Plan a second lander for the same mission that lands on the far side. Say how it will talk to the Earth.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own landing. Draw the calendar. Mark landing day, noon and sunset. Draw what the Moon looks like from India on each of the three days. Why did you pick your day?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about timing. You use the Moon's phases to pick the best day to land a lander that runs on sunlight.

setup.art: A calendar page with the 4th marked as a new Moon, and small Moon shapes drawn on the 11th, 18th and 26th.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the phases on the calendar page.

setup.art: A ball lit by a torch from the side, with a small pin on the ball, showing the pin just coming into the light.
setup.caption: 2. Use a ball and a torch to check when the pin has sunrise.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child what the Moon looks like from India when it is sunrise, noon and sunset at the centre of the near side.
flow.say: A lander only works in sunlight. At the centre of the near side, the Sun rises at first quarter. What does the Moon look like from India when it is noon there? And when it is sunset there?
flow.kid: A lander needs sunlight. When does the Sun rise at the centre? Guess.

ask.q: When will the lander have the most sunlight left?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Land at Lunar Dawn challenge. You read the problem.

flow.do: 1. Draw a calendar for 30 days. 2. Mark the new Moon on the 4th. 3. Mark the first quarter on the 11th, the full Moon on the 18th and the last quarter on the 26th. 4. Draw a small Moon shape beside each.
flow.say: Draw the calendar. Mark the new Moon on the 4th. Count seven days to the half Moon, then seven more to the full Moon, and seven more to the next half Moon.
flow.kid: Draw the calendar. Mark the four main Moons.
flow.parent: Use days 11, 18 and 26. New Moon on the 4th, first quarter about 7 days later on the 11th, full Moon about 14 days later on the 18th, and last quarter about 22 days after the new Moon, on the 26th. The Moon on the 11th is lit on the right when seen from India.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the calendar and mark the phases.

flow.do: 1. Choose a landing day. 2. Mark sunrise, noon and sunset for the lander on the calendar. 3. Count how many days of sunlight are left from the landing day. 4. Write why you chose it.
flow.say: Pick the landing day. Mark sunrise, noon and sunset. How many days of sunlight does the lander have? Write why you chose that day.
flow.kid: Pick a landing day. Mark sunrise, noon and sunset. Count the days.

ask.q: Which day did you choose, and how many days of sunlight does the lander have?
good: The 11th or 12th, so it has about two weeks.

flow.parent: A good answer lands on the 11th to 13th, a day or two after sunrise at the first quarter. Sunset is on the 26th, so the lander has about 14 days. If your child lands at the full Moon, the lander has only about a week left. Use the ball and torch to check.

check.q: Why is landing at the full Moon a poor choice for a lander at the centre of the near side?
options: The Sun is already overhead, and it will set in about a week
The Moon is too far away
check.why: At full Moon the centre of the near side has noon, and sunset comes at the last quarter, about a week later. A lander that needs 14 days of daylight would run out of sun. Picking 'too dark' is the opposite of the truth.

flow.context: In this step, you choose the day and plan the lander's sunlight.

flow.do: Show your plan to someone else. Talk about what the Moon looks like on landing day, and what you would change.
flow.say: Explain your plan to someone. What does the Moon look like on landing day? What would you change for a pole landing?
flow.kid: Tell someone your plan. What does the Moon look like?

check.q: A lander lands near the line between light and dark on a growing half Moon. Where is the Sun in the lander's sky?
options: It has just risen and is low in the sky
check.why: On a growing Moon, the lit side is the side where it is morning. A site near the line has just had its sunrise, so the Sun is low. That is where long shadows fall.

flow.think: Why might scientists choose a landing site where the Sun is always low?
flow.context: In this last step, you explain your plan and think about other sites.

items.p: Put these Moons in order by their age, from the youngest to the oldest.
items.why: The Moon's age counts the days since the new Moon. A thin crescent is a few days old, the first quarter about 7, the full Moon about 15 and the last quarter about 22.

items.p: What is the terminator on the Moon?
opts: The line between the lit part and the dark part
The dark side of the Moon
The edge of the Moon in the sky
items.why: The terminator is the line where the Moon's day meets its night. For a place on the Moon, it is sunrise or sunset. It is not a dark side or a crater.

items.p: Which night is the poorest for seeing craters through binoculars?
items.why: At full Moon, the Sun lights the Moon from behind us, so there are almost no shadows. Craters look flat. The other nights have light from the side.

items.p: The line between the lit and dark parts of the Moon is called the ____.
items.why: On the real Moon, the terminator is the place where it is sunrise or sunset, and shadows there are long.

items.p: At full Moon, the Sun is low in the sky over the middle of the Moon's face.
items.why: False. At full Moon the Sun shines straight down on the middle of the near side, so it is lunar noon there. The Sun is low only near the terminator.

items.p: You light a ball of dough with a torch beside your head, and you see almost no craters. Then you move the torch to the side and see many. Explain what changed.
items.a: With the torch beside your head, the light came from the same direction you were looking, so the craters made almost no shadows and looked flat. With the torch at the side, each crater had a dark shadow on one side, and the shadows showed its shape.
items.why: A strong answer says that shadows show shape, and that light from the side makes long shadows.

items.p: A Moon is 7 days old. What does it look like from India?
opts: A half Moon, lit on the right
A thin crescent lit on the left
items.why: At 7 days old, the Moon is at its first quarter. It is half lit. A growing Moon is lit on its right side when seen from India.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the line between the Moon's day and night
dark flat plains of old lava
a bowl made by a rock from space
the days since the last new Moon
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words are the main ideas of the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Draw a half Moon with a crater near the line between light and dark. Draw its shadow, and show which way the Sun is.
items.a: A half Moon lit on the right, with a crater near the middle line. The shadow inside the crater is on the side facing the dark. An arrow shows the Sun on the lit side.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the shadow on the side away from the Sun.
items.art: A circle with the right half shaded light and the left half dark, with a small oval crater near the middle line.

items.p: Sort these nights into good and poor nights for seeing craters through binoculars.
items.a: see items
items.why: Craters show best when the Sun is low, so near the terminator of a half Moon or a crescent. A new Moon cannot be seen, and a nearly full Moon is lit from behind us.

items.p: Label the diagram of a crater on the Moon: the Sun's direction, the crater's shadow, the lit rim and the dark floor.
items.a: An arrow for the Sun on one side, the lit rim on the side facing the Sun, the shadow and dark floor on the other side.
items.why: The shadow always lies away from the Sun. A strong label puts the lit rim on the Sun's side.
items.art: A bowl-shaped crater cut in half with four blank label lines.

items.p: Two friends in Bengaluru are planning a night to look at the Moon with binoculars.

views.says: I will look at the full Moon, because it is the brightest and I will see the most.
I will look at the half Moon, because the craters have shadows on it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about shadows. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Zainab, because the half Moon is lit from the side and shows craters with shadows, while the full Moon is lit from behind us and looks flat. It gives Meera her due: the full Moon is the brightest and the most beautiful, and it shows bright rays and the dark plains well.
items.why: This tests the main idea: shadows from slanting light show shape, so a brighter Moon is not a better one for craters.

items.p: About how much later does the Moon rise each day?
items.why: The Moon moves round the Earth in the same direction as the Earth spins, so the Earth must turn a little extra to catch up with it each day, about 50 minutes.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Maria, highlands and craters are all parts of the Moon's ground. The terminator is a line between light and dark that moves, and it is not a part of the ground.

items.p: The Sun sets at 6 in the evening, and the Moon is 4 days old. Use the 50-minute rule to say about when it sets, and show your working.
items.a: 4 times 50 minutes is 200 minutes, which is 3 hours and 20 minutes. 6 in the evening plus 3 hours 20 minutes is about 9:20 at night. So it sets at about half past nine.
items.why: A strong answer multiplies the age by 50 minutes and adds it to sunset. It says that the answer is a guide and not exact.

items.p: The Moon's craters are old volcanoes.
items.why: False. Most of the Moon's craters were made by rocks hitting the ground. They are round, with raised rims, and match craters made in tests. The dark plains are old lava, but they are not craters.

worksheets.title: Tides, Distance and the Moon's Day (stretch)

items.p: Why do most coasts have two high tides a day?
opts: The sea bulges on the side facing the Moon and on the opposite side, and the Earth turns under both
The Moon goes round the Earth twice a day
The Sun pushes the sea twice
items.why: The Moon's pull stretches the sea into two bulges. As the Earth turns once under them, a coast meets two high tides. The Moon does not go round twice in a day.

items.p: The gap between two high tides is about 12 hours and ____ minutes.
items.why: The Moon moves on while the Earth turns, so the gap is a little longer than 12 hours. The extra is about 25 minutes.

items.p: When do spring tides happen?
opts: At new Moon and full Moon
items.why: At new Moon and full Moon, the Sun and the Moon pull along the same line and make bigger tides. The name spring has nothing to do with the season.

items.p: Put these tides in the order they come, starting at new Moon.
items.why: Tides are big at new Moon and full Moon and small at the quarters. The rhythm repeats about every two weeks.

items.p: High tide was at 5:30 in the morning on Monday. About when will it be on Tuesday morning, and why is it not the same time?
items.a: About 6:20 in the morning. The tides follow the Moon, and the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, so the high tide comes about 50 minutes later.
items.why: A strong answer adds about 50 minutes and links it to the Moon's movement.

items.p: The ground on the Moon stays warm all night because rock holds heat.
items.why: False. With no air to hold in the heat, the ground cools quickly in the Moon's night and falls to about minus 170 degrees Celsius near the equator.

items.p: A disc 10 millimetres wide just covers the Moon from 1,100 millimetres away. The Moon is ____ of its own widths away.
items.why: 1,100 divided by 10 is 110. A small disc covers the Moon when it is 110 of its own widths from your eye.

items.p: The Moon is about 110 of its widths away, and it is about 384,000 kilometres away. Work out about how wide it is.
items.a: 384,000 divided by 110 is about 3,490 kilometres. So the Moon is about 3,500 kilometres wide, a little wider than India is long.
items.why: A strong answer divides the distance by 110 and says the width is about 3,500 kilometres.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in a line at new Moon. Draw the sea on the Earth with a bulge facing the Moon and a bulge on the other side.
items.a: The Sun on one side, the Moon in the middle, the Earth on the other side, and two bulges of water on the Earth along the line.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the far side.
items.art: A small Sun on the left, an empty space in the middle and a small blue Earth on the right.

items.p: Label the picture of the Moon's day: sunrise, noon, sunset and night.
items.a: Sunrise on the side where the Sun is coming up, noon where the Sun is overhead, sunset on the opposite side from sunrise and night in the dark half.
items.why: Sunrise, noon, sunset and night follow each other round the Moon. A strong label shows the Sun's direction at each point.
items.art: A circle with a Sun on the right and four blank label lines.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru are arguing about the colour of the Moon.

views.says: The Moon is white. I can see it is bright white in the night sky.
The Moon is dark grey. It only reflects a little of the Sun's light, like a tarred road.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Imran: the Moon sends back only about 12 parts in 100 of the sunlight that falls on it, so it is dark grey. It gives Latha her due: it looks white because the night sky around it is black, and she describes what we see.
items.why: This tests whether a child separates what a thing is from how it looks against its surroundings.

items.p: Why was Chandrayaan-3 timed to land at lunar dawn?
opts: So its solar-powered lander would have about two weeks of daylight
Because the Moon is brightest at dawn
Because the Earth is closest at dawn
Because dawn is cooler for the crew
items.why: The lander ran on sunlight and could not survive the cold of the lunar night. Landing just after sunrise gave it about 14 Earth days of sun. There was no crew on board.

items.p: Sort each thing into 'changes with the Moon's age' or 'does not change'.
items: the shape of the lit part
the distance from the Earth to the Sun, in a month
items.a: see items
items.why: The phase, the moonrise time and the size of the tides all follow the Moon's position. The Moon's width does not change, and the Sun's distance hardly changes in a month. A strong answer says why.

items.p: Match each number to what it measures.
pairs: about how long the Moon's daylight lasts at one place
about how much later the Moon rises each day
the time from one new Moon to the next
about how far away the Moon is
about how many Moon-widths away the Moon is
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These numbers come from the experiments and explanations in the unit. A strong answer could say how each was measured.

items.p: Three of these are on the Moon's surface. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Maria, highlands and rays are all things on the Moon's surface. Tides are the movement of the sea on the Earth, caused by the Moon.

items.p: Why can we see about 59 parts out of every 100 of the Moon's surface over time?
opts: The Moon nods and rocks a little, which lets us see round its edges
items.why: The Moon rocks and nods by a few degrees. This is called libration, and it lets us peek a little way round the edges of the face.

items.p: Galileo saw bright specks in the dark part of the Moon, near the line between light and dark. The specks grew and joined the lit part over a few days. What did he guess they were, and why?
items.a: He guessed that they were mountain tops. The Sun had just reached their tops, but not the low ground around them. As the Sun rose higher on the Moon, the light spread down and joined the lit part.
items.why: A strong answer says the tops catch the first light, as hilltops do at dawn on the Earth.

items.p: A mound on a model Moon is 2 centimetres tall and casts a 6 centimetre shadow. What can you say about the light?
opts: It is coming in at a low angle
It is coming from straight overhead
It is coming from straight behind the viewer
items.why: A shadow three times as long as the mound means the light is low, so the angle is shallow. Light from straight overhead would make almost no shadow.

items.p: Two friends want to photograph craters on the Moon with a phone and binoculars.

views.says: We should wait for the quarter Moon, since the craters show up near the line between day and night.
We should photograph the full Moon, since there is more light and the photo will be sharper.

items.ask: Who has the better plan? Say why. Then say one good thing about the other plan.
items.a: A strong answer picks Sneha's plan, because shadows along the terminator show shape. It gives Rahul his due: a full Moon is bright, so a short exposure is easy, and the photo can show the bright rays and dark plains well. Neither plan involves looking at the Sun.
items.why: This is a real trade-off between brightness and detail. Both give something.

items.p: In the Dough Moon experiment, someone counted 8 craters and lumps with the torch beside their head and only 3 with the torch at the side. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The torch was not low enough at the side, or the craters were shallow
The Moon is made of dough
items.why: Shadows from the side show shape only if the torch is low and the craters are deep. If the side light is too high, there are few shadows. A good scientist checks that the test was done properly before doubting the idea.

items.p: Put these steps in order for predicting tonight's Moon.
items: Multiply the age by 50 minutes to guess when it sets or rises
Use the age to name the phase and the lit side
Count the days since then to get the Moon's age
Find the date of the last new Moon
a: Find the date of the last new Moon
Count the days since then to get the Moon's age
Use the age to name the phase and the lit side
Multiply the age by 50 minutes to guess when it sets or rises
items.why: You need the age before you can find the phase, and the phase before you can describe the shape. The time rule uses the age too. A strong answer follows this order.

items.p: The gap between moonrises in a table is sometimes 40 minutes and sometimes 65 minutes. Explain why the rule 'about 50 minutes' is still useful.
items.a: On average the gap is about 50 minutes, even though single nights vary. The Moon's speed and the angle of its path change a little through the month. The rule gives a good guess for planning, but not an exact time.
items.why: A strong answer says the rule is an average and that real nights vary a little.

items.p: Everyone in the world who can see the Moon sees it lit on the same side.
items.why: False. The phase is the same for everyone, but the side that is lit depends on where you are. In India a growing Moon is lit on the right. In Australia it is lit on the left.

items.p: Draw a growing half Moon as it looks from Australia, and say which side is lit.
items.a: A half Moon lit on the left. The lit side faces the Sun, but the Moon appears upside down compared with India.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lit side on the left, and the reason is that the viewer is in the southern half of the world.
items.art: A blank circle with the words 'Australia' and 'growing half Moon' written beside it.

items.p: Label the Earth, the Moon and the two tidal bulges. Show which way the Earth turns.
items.a: The Earth in the middle, two bulges of water along the line to the Moon, the Moon on one side and a curved arrow showing the Earth's spin.
items.why: The bulges stay lined up with the Moon while the Earth turns. A strong label shows both bulges.
items.art: A circle for the Earth, a small circle for the Moon at the right and four blank label lines.

items.p: Why is there a tidal bulge on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon?
opts: The Moon's pull is weaker there than on the rest of the Earth, so the sea is left behind
The Moon pushes the sea away
items.why: The Moon's pull gets weaker with distance. The solid Earth is pulled more than the water on the far side, so the far side water is left behind and heaps up.

items.p: The Moon sends back only about 12 parts in every 100 of the sunlight that falls on it. Explain why it still looks bright at night.
items.a: The Moon reflects enough sunlight to be seen, and the night sky around it is dark. Our eyes judge brightness by comparison, so it looks bright against black.
items.why: A strong answer says brightness is judged against the surroundings.

items.p: The Moon sends back about ____ parts of every 100 parts of the sunlight that fall on it.
items.why: About 12 percent is reflected. The Moon's rocks are dark grey, about as dark as a tarred road.

items.p: You see a thin crescent low in the western sky just after sunset. Where is the Sun?
opts: Just below the horizon in the west, below the crescent
items.why: The Moon's lit side always faces the Sun. A crescent just after sunset is lit on the side towards the setting Sun, which is just below the western horizon.

items.p: A friend says moonlight is almost as bright as sunlight, because a full Moon is so bright. How would you answer?
items.a: The full Moon is about 400,000 times fainter than the Sun. It seems bright only because our eyes have adjusted to the dark.
items.why: A strong answer gives the big difference between the Moon's and the Sun's brightness and says why it seems bright.

items.p: A crater at the Moon's pole has a floor that never sees the Sun. Why might it hold ice?
opts: It is always extremely cold, so ice could last for billions of years
items.why: Near the poles, the Sun is always low. Deep crater walls shade the floor all the time. With no sunlight and no air, it stays extremely cold, and any ice that got there could stay.

quiz.p: Which of these best describes the terminator on the Moon?
opts: The line where the Moon's day meets its night
The edge of the Moon's disc
quiz.why: The terminator is the moving line between the lit and dark parts of the Moon. There, the Sun is rising or setting.

quiz.p: Why do the long shadows along the terminator help us?
opts: They show the shape of craters and mountains
quiz.why: Low sunlight makes long shadows. We read the shape of rough ground by its shadows.

quiz.p: Which Moon is a poor choice for seeing craters?
quiz.why: At full Moon, the Sun lights the Moon from behind us. The craters make almost no shadows, so they look flat.

quiz.p: A friend says the full Moon is the best for seeing craters because it is brightest. What is wrong?
opts: Light from straight behind us makes almost no shadows
The full Moon is farther away
quiz.why: Brightness is not the same as seeing detail. Shadows show shape, and a full Moon has almost none.

quiz.p: A Moon is 22 days old. What does it look like from India?
opts: A half Moon lit on the left
A half Moon lit on the right
quiz.why: At 22 days it is the last quarter. A shrinking Moon is lit on the left when seen from India.

quiz.p: The Sun sets at 6 pm and the Moon is 7 days old. About when does the Moon set?
quiz.why: Seven times 50 minutes is about 6 hours. Six hours after 6 pm is midnight.

quiz.p: How long is the sunlit part of a lunar day at a place near the Moon's equator?
quiz.why: A full day on the Moon lasts about 29 and a half Earth days, so the daylight lasts about two weeks and the night about two weeks.

quiz.p: Why does the Moon's ground get so cold at night?
opts: There is no air to hold in the heat
The Moon is far from the Sun
quiz.why: Without air, heat escapes quickly after sunset. The ground falls to about minus 170 degrees Celsius.

quiz.p: A small disc just covers the Moon at about 110 times its own width from your eye. What does this tell you?
opts: The Moon is about 110 of its own widths away
The Moon is 110 times bigger than the disc
quiz.why: A small disc close to the eye can cover a large thing far away if they are in the same proportion. The ratio of distance to width is the same for both.

quiz.p: Why are there two high tides a day on most coasts?
opts: The sea bulges towards the Moon and away from it, and the Earth turns under both
The Moon goes round the Earth twice a day
The tides slosh back and forth
quiz.why: The Moon's pull makes two bulges in the sea. The Earth turns once a day under them, so a place meets two high tides.

opts: A day or two after new Moon and full Moon
quiz.why: At new Moon and full Moon, the Sun and the Moon pull along one line, so their pulls add up.

quiz.p: Galileo noticed bright specks in the dark part of the Moon near the terminator. What did he decide they were?
opts: Mountain tops catching the first sunlight
quiz.why: The tops of the Moon's mountains are lit first at sunrise, before the valleys. Galileo understood this from the way the specks grew and joined the light.

open_questions.q: How much water ice is there in the Moon's shadowed craters, and can we use it?
open_questions.why_open: Several spacecraft have found signs of ice, but only a few have landed near the poles. How much there is and how deep it lies are still being measured.

open_questions.q: Why are the Moon's near and far sides so different?
open_questions.why_open: The near side has big dark plains, and the far side has hardly any. Scientists have several ideas, such as the young Earth's heat or a giant crash, but none is settled.

open_questions.q: How long will the Moon keep moving away from the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: The Moon drifts away by a few centimetres each year. How this will change over billions of years depends on the oceans, and scientists are still working it out.

open_questions.q: What was the Moon's surface like when it was young, and when did the big impacts stop?
open_questions.why_open: Rocks brought back by astronauts give ages for craters, but we have rock from only a few places. Scientists argue about whether there was a late burst of impacts.

open_questions.q: Did tides in the Earth's early oceans help life to begin?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists suggest that pools on the shore, wetted and dried by the tides again and again, could have helped to build the first chemicals of life. There is no firm evidence yet.

open_questions.q: Could people live and work in the permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles?
open_questions.why_open: The cold is extreme, and the ground has never been seen up close. Engineers and scientists are still working out whether people could use it.

maths.problem: A bindi 7 millimetres wide just covers the Moon when it is 770 millimetres from your eye. How many Moon-widths away is the Moon? The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away. About how wide is it?
maths.answer: The Moon is 110 of its widths away, so it is about 3,490 kilometres wide.
maths.explain: 770 divided by 7 is 110. 384,000 divided by 110 is about 3,490. So the Moon is about 3,500 kilometres wide.
maths.context: In the Bindi Moon, you stick a bindi on a window glass and find where it exactly covers the Moon.
maths.why_maths: We cannot put a ruler across the Moon. Dividing two measurements we can make at home tells us the Moon's real width.

maths.problem: A new Moon was on the 2nd of the month. What is the Moon's age on the 17th? Is it near a half Moon, a full Moon or a crescent?
maths.answer: 15 days old, which is a full Moon.
maths.explain: 17 take away 2 is 15. A Moon that is 15 days old is about full.
maths.why_maths: Counting the days since the last new Moon gives the age, and the age tells you the phase.

maths.problem: In the moonrise table, the gaps between days were 48, 52, 55, 50 and 45 minutes. What is the average gap?
maths.explain: 48 plus 52 is 100. 100 plus 55 is 155. 155 plus 50 is 205. 205 plus 45 is 250. 250 divided by 5 is 50.
maths.context: In Moonrise Detective, you find the gap between the Moon's rise times on ten days in a row.
maths.why_maths: An average turns several different gaps into one number we can use as a rule.

maths.problem: The Sun rises at 6:10 in the morning. The Moon is 14 days old. Use the rule of 50 minutes for each day of the Moon's age to say about when the Moon rises.
maths.explain: 14 times 50 is 700 minutes. 700 minutes is 11 hours and 40 minutes. 6:10 in the morning plus 11 hours 40 minutes is 5:50 in the evening.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the age by the daily gap lets us guess the moonrise, then check it with the sky.

maths.problem: The Moon's ground is about 120 degrees Celsius at midday and about minus 170 degrees Celsius at night. How many degrees is the difference?
maths.explain: From minus 170 up to 0 is 170. From 0 up to 120 is 120. 170 plus 120 is 290.
maths.why_maths: Negative numbers let us measure how far the Moon's temperature swings from its coldest to its hottest.

maths.problem: High tide is at 5:30 in the morning today. Each day it is about 50 minutes later. When will it be 4 days from now?
maths.explain: 4 times 50 is 200 minutes, which is 3 hours and 20 minutes. 5:30 plus 3 hours 20 minutes is 8:50.
maths.context: In Tide Detective, you read a tide table over fifteen days.
maths.why_maths: Repeating a daily shift is how tide tables and moonrise tables can be predicted.

maths.problem: In a model, the Earth is a ball 2 centimetres wide. The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth, and about 30 Earth-widths away. How wide is the Moon ball, and how far from the Earth ball?
maths.answer: The Moon ball is 0.5 centimetres wide, and 60 centimetres away.
maths.explain: A quarter of 2 centimetres is 0.5 centimetres. 30 times 2 centimetres is 60 centimetres.
maths.why_maths: A scale model shows how far apart the Earth and the Moon really are, which a normal picture cannot.

maths.problem: The Moon sends back 12 parts in every 100 of the sunlight that falls on it. If 500 units of sunlight fall on a patch of Moon, how many units are sent back?
maths.explain: 12 out of 100 is 12 percent. 500 divided by 100 is 5. 5 times 12 is 60.
maths.why_maths: Percentages show how dark the Moon is, even though it looks bright in the night sky.

maths.problem: A mound 2 centimetres tall makes a shadow 3 centimetres long on a dough Moon. In the same light, another mound makes a 6 centimetre shadow. How tall is it?
maths.explain: The shadow is 1 and a half times the height. 6 divided by 3 is 2, so the second shadow is twice as long. So the mound is twice as tall, 2 times 2 is 4 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Dough Moon, you light lumps from the side and measure the length of their shadows.
maths.why_maths: In the same light, a mound's height and its shadow stay in the same proportion, so a shadow can measure a height.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Dough Moon needs only dough, a torch and a dark room. Press the craters deep with a katori rim, keep the torch low at the side, and keep the plate in one place. The counts will vary, so write down what you saw. Moonrise Detective needs a phone, newspaper or panchang with moonrise times for your city, ideally for ten days in a row starting two days after a new Moon. Single gaps may run from about 30 to about 70 minutes. The Bindi Moon needs the Moon to be visible from a window, and works with a bindi 5 to 8 millimetres wide. Pick a night when the Moon is easy to see. If the Moon is not visible, try another night. Never use this on the Sun. Catch Up works on any table with a lamp, an orange and a lime. Tide Detective needs a tide table for a port, from a newspaper or a website. If the pattern is unclear, use fifteen days. The Terminator Log depends on clear evenings. Binoculars are used after sunset only, and a grown-up should come to the terrace.
